entityAttributes.origins: Self-sovereign identity plus payment rails — created on the premise that SSI adoption was constrained by the absence of a sustainable commercial model for issuers and verifiers, and that identity infrastructure needed native payment and incentive mechanisms to reach scale [b]
entityAttributes.database: cheqd network — a Cosmos SDK blockchain with CometBFT consensus, storing DID documents and DID-Linked Resources on-chain [b][c]
entityAttributes.queryLanguage: cheqd DID Resolver (resolver.cheqd.net) and the DIF Universal Resolver; DID-Linked Resources are queryable by resourceName, resourceType, resourceVersion and resourceVersionTime, giving time-travel access to prior versions [b][c]
entityAttributes.dataFormats: W3C DID Document (JSON/JSON-LD); DID-Linked Resources as sequentially ordered, indexable and historically queryable JSON files with resourceName / resourceType / resourceVersion metadata and optional alternativeUri [b][c]
entityAttributes.mobileSupport: Library-level — implemented inside resolver libraries and wallets; no standalone application [a]
entityAttributes.webSupport: Yes — public HTTPS resolution via resolver.cheqd.net and the DIF Universal Resolver, in addition to direct chain reads [b][c]
entityAttributes.nativeApps: Library-level — embedded in resolver libraries; no standalone application [a]
entityAttributes.terms: Transaction fees in CHEQ for writes; reads and resolution are free via public resolvers. Commercial payment flows for credential services are an explicit design feature rather than an incidental cost [b]
entityAttributes.funds: Unknown — figures not confirmed in the sources reviewed [b]
entityAttributes.basedOn: W3C DID Core 1.0; Cosmos SDK and CometBFT consensus; W3C DID-Linked Resources specification (W3C CCG); interoperates with the ToIP did:scid method as a named DID host option [b][c]
entityAttributes.authenticationIdentity: Ledger-anchored with clear separation between the identity keypair and the blockchain keypair — the account that pays for and submits a transaction need not be the DID controller, a design the ToIP did:scid specification cites approvingly as an ADR-documented pattern [b][c]
entityAttributes.storageModel: On-chain — DID documents and DID-Linked Resources stored on the cheqd network, replicated across validators. The DID-Linked Resource mechanism provides versioned, historically queryable storage functioning as a microledger for resource updates [b][c]
entityAttributes.interoperability: W3C DID ecosystem via the cheqd resolver and the DIF Universal Resolver; supports W3C Verifiable Credentials and AnonCreds; named in the ToIP did:scid specification as a blockchain DID host, where a did:scid identifier can point to verification metadata anchored on cheqd [b][c]
entityAttributes.dataPortability: Chain-bound — identifiers and resources live on the cheqd network and cannot be migrated to another chain or method without re-issuance. The did:scid integration is explicitly an attempt to decouple identifier from location, which is an acknowledgement of this limitation [b][c]
entityAttributes.governanceDecisionMaking: On-chain token-holder governance — CHEQ holders vote on network parameters and upgrades through Cosmos governance modules, with CHEQD FOUNDATION LIMITED as the principal contributing organization [a][b]
entityAttributes.identityStandards: W3C DID Core 1.0; W3C Verifiable Credentials; AnonCreds support; W3C DID-Linked Resources; registered in the W3C DID Extensions methods registry [a][b][c]
entityAttributes.didMethodsSupported: did:cheqd (defines this method), with testnet and mainnet namespaces. Serves as a host for did:scid identifiers via DID-Linked Resources [a][b][c]
entityAttributes.keyManagement: Controller-managed with on-chain rotation — verification method updates are submitted as signed transactions, giving an auditable on-chain history. The DID controller keypair is deliberately distinct from the blockchain account keypair [b][c]
entityAttributes.credentialTypes: N/A — a DID method specification; defines no credential types. Compatible with W3C Verifiable Credentials issued against identifiers of this method [a]
entityAttributes.verificationMethod: Resolution from the cheqd chain, with correctness resting on CometBFT consensus. DID-Linked Resources may be signed with keys from the DID document's authentication section, providing cryptographic verifiability back to the controller [b][c]
entityAttributes.privacyFeatures: Standard for a public chain — DID documents are publicly readable, so pairwise privacy must come from using a different method for holder identifiers. AnonCreds support provides selective disclosure at the credential layer. Payment flows introduce their own metadata surface [b]
entityAttributes.authenticationMethods: Cryptographic signature against verification methods recorded on-chain [b]
entityAttributes.revocationMechanism: On-chain DID deactivation; credential revocation via status lists or AnonCreds revocation registries published as DID-Linked Resources, with version history preserved [b][c]
entityAttributes.agentTypesSupported: Any key-controlling entity — individuals, organizations, services and devices [a]
entityAttributes.walletClientTypes: SDK / library integration — resolver implementations across the SSI tooling ecosystem; no method-specific wallet [a]
entityAttributes.recoveryMechanisms: Key rotation by the current controller; multi-key and multi-controller configurations possible via the DID document. No social or custodial recovery defined at the method level [b]
entityAttributes.complianceRegulations: Positioned for regulated commercial use — a named UK legal entity, published governance, and payment rails designed with compliance in mind. The token component conversely introduces securities and financial-regulatory exposure [b]
entityAttributes.credentialExchangeProtocols: DIDComm, OpenID4VC, and AnonCreds presentation exchange; resolver support in the DIF Universal Resolver makes it usable by any W3C DID-resolving protocol [b][c]
entityAttributes.trustFramework: Ledger consensus plus commercial accountability — cryptographic verification against chain state, combined with an identifiable corporate entity and on-chain governance. Trust registries are a first-class supported use case [b][c]
entityAttributes.costModel: Paid — CHEQ-denominated transaction fees for writes, with the payment layer for credential issuance and verification being the network's deliberate differentiator. Reads and resolution are free [b]
entityAttributes.censorshipResistance: Moderate — writes are permissionless (anyone holding CHEQ can create a DID, unlike Indy's endorser model) and the validator set is independent, but the chain has a single identifiable corporate sponsor and a token whose availability could be constrained by exchange or regulatory action [a][b]
entityAttributes.protocolMaturityStandardization: Registered W3C DID method with a live mainnet, public resolver, DIF Universal Resolver support, and third-party specification uptake — the ToIP did:scid method devotes an appendix to cheqd as a DID host. Method specification is a project ADR rather than a standards-body document [a][b][c]
entityAttributes.permissions: Cryptographic key control for DID updates; chain-level permissionless write subject to fee payment; DID-Linked Resource publication authorised by the DID's authentication keys [b][c]

name: did:ethr
description: The DID method for Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains, built on the ERC-1056 lightweight identity registry. Its defining property is that any Ethereum address is already a valid did:ethr identifier with no transaction required — the DID document is derived from the address by default and only needs on-chain writes if the controller wants to rotate keys, add delegates or attach service endpoints, which are recorded as registry events rather than stored documents. Resolution replays those events to reconstruct current state. Originating in the uPort project and now maintained through Veramo and the DIF ecosystem, it is the most widely used identity method across EVM chains. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Active — registered in the W3C DID Extensions methods registry (registry: 'Ethereum'). ethr-did-resolver is a mature, widely used library supported in the DIF Universal Resolver; the registry contract is deployed across Ethereum mainnet and numerous EVM chains. Notably, it is the resolver that Verida's did:vda originally forked before replacing it [a][b][c]
owner: Decentralized Identity Foundation ecosystem — specification contact listed in the W3C registry is Mircea Nistor. Lineage runs from uPort through Consensys Mesh to the Veramo project; the ethr-did-registry contract and ethr-did-resolver are community-maintained [a][b][c]
governingBody: DIF (resolver maintenance) | Ethereum EIP/ERC process (ERC-1056) | None (the deployed registry contract is immutable with no admin key or upgrade path)
country: International — contributor base spans Europe and the USA; the underlying chains are jurisdiction-independent [a][b]
stack: Solidity (ERC-1056 EthereumDIDRegistry contract); TypeScript/JavaScript (ethr-did-resolver, ethr-did); resolver implementations in other languages available [b][c]
license: Permissive (Apache-2.0) — ethr-did-resolver and ethr-did libraries at https://github.com/decentralized-identity/ethr-did-resolver; ERC-1056 registry contract published openly [b][c]
funding: Community-maintained — originally funded through uPort/Consensys; now maintained by DIF community contributors and the Veramo project. No dedicated funding entity [b][c]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2). Governance & legal control (≈2): ERC-1056 is a published open standard and the resolver is Apache-2.0 under the DIF GitHub organization; the registry contract is immutable once deployed and has no admin key or upgrade path, so no party can alter its behaviour after deployment [a][b][c]. Funding & key-org dependency (≈2): the original uPort/Consensys sponsorship has wound down and maintenance now sits with the DIF community and Veramo contributors; the contract itself requires no funding to keep operating, which decouples the method's survival from any organization's continued interest [b][c]. Forking viability (≈2): the standard and resolver are trivially forkable and the contract is already deployed across many chains, though existing identifiers remain bound to their deployment [b]. Regulatory / jurisdictional exposure (≈2): no native token and no legal entity attached to the method; exposure is whatever attaches to the underlying chain [b]. Track record (≈1): no capture events across roughly eight years; the abandoned-sponsor risk has already materialised without breaking the method, which is itself evidence of resilience [b][c]

references.note: W3C DID Extensions methods registry entry for 'ethr': registry 'Ethereum', contact Mircea Nistor (verified 2026-07-28)
did:ethr method specification and resolver (Apache-2.0, DIF): ERC-1056 registry, event-replay resolution, default document derivation, delegates and attributes, chain namespacing
ERC-1056 Ethereum Lightweight Identity (Pelle Braendgaard, Joel Torstensson, uPort, 2018): registry contract design, owner and delegate model, gas-free default identity

entityAttributes.origins: Ethereum identity / uPort — created to give every Ethereum account a usable decentralized identifier without requiring a transaction or new infrastructure, addressing the cost and friction of on-chain identity registration [b][c]
entityAttributes.database: ERC-1056 EthereumDIDRegistry smart contract — an event-log-based registry rather than a document store; DID documents are reconstructed by replaying DIDOwnerChanged, DIDDelegateChanged and DIDAttributeChanged events [b][c]
entityAttributes.queryLanguage: Ethereum JSON-RPC event log queries — the resolver reads registry events for the address and replays them; no separate query language [b][c]
entityAttributes.dataFormats: W3C DID Document reconstructed from registry events; identifier is an Ethereum address with an optional chain namespace (did:ethr:<chain>:0x...); attributes encoded as bytes32 keys in registry events [b][c]
entityAttributes.mobileSupport: Library-level — implemented inside resolver libraries and wallets; no standalone application [a]
entityAttributes.webSupport: Library-level — resolution runs over Ethereum JSON-RPC; the DIF Universal Resolver additionally exposes an HTTPS endpoint [b][c]
entityAttributes.nativeApps: Library-level — embedded in resolver libraries; no standalone application [a]
entityAttributes.terms: Free to create and resolve — an unregistered address resolves to a valid default DID document at zero cost. Gas fees apply only for optional on-chain updates such as key rotation, delegate addition or service endpoints [b][c]
entityAttributes.funds: N/A — no funding entity attached to the method; the deployed contract has no operating cost [b]
entityAttributes.basedOn: W3C DID Core 1.0; ERC-1056 Ethereum Lightweight Identity Registry; Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains; secp256k1 key material. Ancestor of Verida's did:vda, which began as a fork of ethr-did-resolver [b][c]
entityAttributes.authenticationIdentity: Address-derived by default, with optional on-chain delegation — control begins as possession of the Ethereum private key, and can be extended through registry-recorded owner changes and delegate assignments, allowing key rotation without changing the identifier [b][c]
entityAttributes.storageModel: On-chain event log — no DID document is stored anywhere; state is derived by replaying registry events. Unmodified identifiers require no storage at all [b][c]
entityAttributes.interoperability: Broad EVM coverage — the registry contract is deployed on Ethereum mainnet and many EVM chains, with a chain namespace in the identifier; supported in the DIF Universal Resolver, Veramo, and most EVM-oriented SSI tooling. Compatible with W3C VCs and EIP-4361 sign-in flows [b][c]
entityAttributes.dataPortability: Chain-bound — an identifier includes its chain namespace, so it cannot be moved between chains without becoming a different DID, though the same underlying key can control identifiers on several chains [b][c]
entityAttributes.governanceDecisionMaking: Open standard with immutable deployment — ERC-1056 went through the public EIP process; the deployed registry contract has no admin function, no owner and no upgrade mechanism, so governance over existing identifiers is effectively absent by construction. Resolver maintenance is community-governed under DIF [b][c]
entityAttributes.identityStandards: W3C DID Core 1.0; ERC-1056; compatible with W3C Verifiable Credentials and EIP-4361 (Sign-In with Ethereum, already on the SCS tab in this file); registered in the W3C DID Extensions methods registry [a][b][c]
entityAttributes.didMethodsSupported: did:ethr (defines this method), with chain-namespaced variants across EVM networks [a][b]
entityAttributes.keyManagement: On-chain rotation and delegation — owner changes and time-bounded delegates are recorded as registry events, giving verifiable key history without changing the identifier. This is the principal advantage over deriving identity from a raw address alone [b][c]
entityAttributes.credentialTypes: N/A — a DID method specification; defines no credential types. Compatible with W3C Verifiable Credentials issued against identifiers of this method [a]
entityAttributes.verificationMethod: Event replay against the chain — the resolver reconstructs the current document from registry history, with correctness resting on the underlying chain's consensus. Default documents require no chain read of registry state beyond confirming absence of events [b][c]
entityAttributes.privacyFeatures: Weak — an Ethereum address is a public, highly correlatable identifier already linked to on-chain financial activity, and any registry updates are permanently public. Pairwise use is possible by generating fresh addresses, but the method offers no privacy features of its own [b]
entityAttributes.authenticationMethods: secp256k1 signature by the controlling key or an authorised delegate; commonly paired with EIP-4361 Sign-In with Ethereum for session authentication [b][c]
entityAttributes.revocationMechanism: Registry events — delegates are time-bounded and expire automatically; owner changes supersede prior control; attribute revocation is recorded as an event. Full history remains publicly auditable [b][c]
entityAttributes.agentTypesSupported: Any key-controlling entity — individuals, organizations, services and devices [a]
entityAttributes.walletClientTypes: SDK / library integration — resolver implementations across the SSI tooling ecosystem; no method-specific wallet [a]
entityAttributes.recoveryMechanisms: Owner transfer via the registry — the current owner can assign a new owner, enabling recovery patterns including multisig or smart-contract-account control. If the controlling key is lost with no prior delegation, no recovery is possible [b][c]
entityAttributes.complianceRegulations: Not addressed by the method. Public correlatability of Ethereum addresses is a material consideration under data-protection regimes, since an address plus registry history is durable, non-erasable personal data where it maps to an individual [b]
entityAttributes.credentialExchangeProtocols: DIDComm, OpenID4VC, and any W3C DID-resolving protocol; widely used with Veramo tooling and with EIP-4361 web sign-in flows [b][c]
entityAttributes.trustFramework: Blockchain consensus with no administrator — the registry contract is immutable and permissionless, so there is no operator, foundation or governance body able to alter or revoke identifiers [b][c]
entityAttributes.costModel: Free for creation and resolution of default identifiers; gas fees on the host chain for optional updates. Cost varies with chain, which is why EVM L2 deployments are common [b][c]
entityAttributes.censorshipResistance: High — the registry contract is immutable with no admin key, resolution is a permissionless chain read, and default identifiers require no transaction at all, so there is nothing to block. Constrained only by access to a node or RPC endpoint for the host chain [b][c]
entityAttributes.protocolMaturityStandardization: Registered W3C DID method built on a published ERC, with roughly eight years of production use, mature Apache-2.0 tooling, and DIF Universal Resolver support. The method specification is a community document rather than a W3C Recommendation; ERC-1056 is the more formal artifact [a][b][c]
entityAttributes.permissions: Cryptographic and delegation-based — owner key controls the identifier; delegates may be granted time-bounded authority for specific purposes, all recorded on-chain [b][c]

name: Keyhive
description: Local-first access control library providing convergent capabilities (concap), group management CRDTs, and end-to-end encryption with causal key management (BeeKEM) for CRDT-based collaborative applications. Designed as a foundational authorization layer beneath identity — enables secure collaboration with read/write/admin roles, coordination-free revocation, and trust-minimized sync servers without requiring a central authority. Targets Automerge ecosystem but designed to be general-purpose for local-first applications [a][b][c].

entityAttributes.credentialTypes: Convergent capabilities (concap): stateful, CRDT-based capability tokens that sit between object-capabilities and certificate-capabilities; delegation chains with read/write/admin/pull access effects; group membership as implicit credential [a]

name: Affinidi
description: A Temasek-founded (2020) data and identity management company building open-standard-based developer infrastructure for consent-driven, privacy-preserving credential issuance, verification, and data sharing. Products include the Affinidi Trust Development Kit (TDK, open source), Affinidi Vault (personal data store), and Affinidi Iota Framework (consent-based selective data sharing via OID4VP). Active pilots include Singapore-India cross-border employment verification (Dec 2025) and cross-border trade interoperability with IMDA. ⚠️ Governance flag: entirely Temasek-controlled (sovereign wealth fund); not community-governed. name: Human Passport
description: A Sybil resistance and proof-of-personhood identity toolkit (formerly Gitcoin Passport) that aggregates identity Stamps — verifiable credentials from multiple Web2 and Web3 identity providers — and computes a Unique Humanity Score for each user. Applications integrate Human Passport to gate access, protect rewards, and ensure governance participation is limited to unique humans. Originally built by Gitcoin to protect quadratic funding rounds; acquired by Holonym Foundation in February 2025 and integrated into the human.tech suite, with credentials migrating toward ZK proof-based verification via the Human Network. Over 2.1M users and 34.5M+ credentials issued; helped distribute $225M+ in grants and airdrops. [a][b][c]

name: Flowsta
description: A self-sovereign identity toolkit built on Holochain providing a 'Sign in with Flowsta' OAuth 2.0 + PKCE authentication layer that gives every user a W3C-compliant Decentralized Identifier (DID) and zero-knowledge encrypted data storage. name: OpenVTC
description: Open Verifiable Trust Community CLI tool implementing the First Person Project white paper to establish 'Know Your Developer' (KYD) trust relationships within open-source developer communities. Uses Decentralised Identifiers (DIDs), Verifiable Credentials (VCs), Personhood Credentials (PHCs), and Verifiable Relationship Credentials (VRCs) to enable verifiable first-person trust relationships among contributors as a defense against supply-chain attacks like the Jia Tan / XZ Utils incident. Reference implementation of the FPP architecture [a][b].
devStatus: Alpha (CLI binary installable from source via cargo; setup wizard, DID generation, DIDComm mediator connectivity, and VRC exchange flows present; no published releases yet; 4 GitHub stars, 6 forks as of May 2026) [a]

name: First Person Project / Network
description: Decentralized proof of personhood infrastructure using Personhood Credentials (PHCs) and Verifiable Relationship Credentials (VRCs) to prove real unique humans with authentic first-person trust relationships, forming a privacy-preserving decentralized trust graph. No centralized database — all credentials stored in user digital wallets. Sparked by the August 2024 Personhood Credentials paper in response to generative AI's ability to impersonate humans. First real-world pilot: Linux Kernel project (kernel.org) to prevent supply chain attacks like the Jia Tan/XZ Utils incident [a][b][c]
devStatus: Early Implementation/Standardization (Decentralized Trust Graph Working Group (DTGWG) established as joint ToIP-DIF Working Group for standardization; Linux Kernel pilot underway; trust communities being recruited; FPNC digital cooperative being established) [a][b][c]
devStatusNote: Early Implementation/Standardization (Decentralized Trust Graph Working Group (DTGWG) established as joint ToIP-DIF Working Group for standardization; Linux Kernel pilot underway; trust communities being recruited; FPNC digital cooperative being established) [a][b][c]
owner: First Person Project (multi-stakeholder collaboration led by Drummond Reed); collaborating LF projects: LF Decentralized Trust (LFDT), Trust Over IP (ToIP), Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF), and OpenWallet Foundation (OWF); additional partners: Ayra Association, Customer Commons; planned: First Person Network Cooperative (FPNC) as governing digital cooperative [a][b][c]
governingBody: Multi-stakeholder consortium (LF Decentralized Trust, ToIP, DIF, OpenWallet Foundation, Ayra Association and Customer Commons; planned First Person Network entity)
stack: Implementation-dependent (builds on Trust Over IP (ToIP) four-layer stack modeled after TCP/IP; Trust Spanning Protocol (TSP) as keystone protocol; LFDT components; zero-knowledge proof cryptography architecture being developed by LFDT CTO Hart Montgomery and Berkeley professor Dr. Sanjam Garg) [a][b][c]
license: Open source (built on open standards: W3C DID, W3C VC, ToIP stack, Trust Spanning Protocol; specific implementations via LFDT components; licenses TBD) [a][b]
funding: Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust (LFDT) as organizational home; collaborating foundations: ToIP, DIF, OWF, Ayra Association, Customer Commons [a][b][c]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Minimal (1): a multi-foundation collaboration built on open standards with no single controlling entity. Governance & legal control (≈1): a multi-stakeholder collaboration across the Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust, ToIP, DIF, and OpenWallet Foundation, built on open W3C and ToIP standards; Drummond Reed leads, but governance sits across multiple foundations [a][b]. Funding & key-org dependency (≈2): organizationally housed at LF Decentralized Trust with multiple collaborating foundations (ToIP, DIF, OWF, Ayra, Customer Commons), diversifying dependence, with a self-sustaining FPNC planned [a][c]. name: GreenCheck
description: A proof-of-personhood and web-of-trust identity system using three-friend authentication and intersectional identity to enable high-trust networks. Each human gets one and only one GreenCheck ID (GCID), forming nodes in a trust graph where validated relationships form edges. Designed as infrastructure for Networked Adaptive Organisms (NAOs) — trust-network-based DAOs for emergent coordination [a][b].

description: A privacy-first social identity network proposing a novel approach to proof-of-uniqueness: each person builds a social graph of connections with people who know them, and Sybil resistance is achieved by analyzing that graph rather than via government ID, biometrics, or centralized verification. Fake identities are detected algorithmically by examining the structure of the connection graph using tools like SybilRank and the Aura algorithm. Applications integrate BrightID to ensure each user holds only one account, enabling fair access to public goods, quadratic voting, and community resources. [a][b][c]

name: XID
description: Novel decentralized identifier architecture — "eXtensible IDentifier" — defined as a unique 32-byte identifier for a subject entity (person, organization, device, or any abstract subject), generated from the SHA-256 hash of an inception key. XIDs resolve to XID Documents — Gordian-Envelope-encoded controller documents that bind the identifier to public keys, permissions, endpoints, and delegation rules — and inherit Envelopes selective elision so the controller document can be tailored per-recipient. The defining architectural insight is that holders, not issuers, control which parts of the controller document are revealed to which counterparties. Intentionally not W3C DID-conformant: XIDs are research/architectural exploration positioned alongside (not within) the W3C DID paradigm. Recently extended with "Edges" (BCR-2026-003) to support web-of-trust attestations between XIDs [a][b][c][d]

name: Common Graph
description: Foundational architecture proposal — "Frames All the Way Down" — for a peer-to-peer network in which every assertion is a signed semantic frame, every coherent thing is an item, and the network is organized by trust rather than servers. The proposal rests on two pillars: (1) a semantic commons grounded in fifty years of computational linguistics (WordNet, CILI, FrameNet, VerbNet) used as the substrates data model — keys are grounded meanings rather than strings, with meaning resolved at write time by the asserter; (2) a peer-to-peer layer in which trust drives routing, moderation, replication, code execution, and discovery — generalized from the PGP web of trust. Structural properties claimed include peer review on every public assertion, moderation as views rather than policy, applications interchangeable on shared data, and software distributed through a trust graph rather than a registry. Note: domain specificity criterion read broadly here — Common Graphs primary contribution is to the data + trust layer rather than to identity strictly, but the architectural-proposal-with-paper-and-early-implementation profile maps cleanly onto ID Sys [a][b][c]

name: XCM
description: Cross-Consensus Messaging Format: a universal, versioned message format for expressing instructions between heterogeneous consensus systems (parachains, relay chains, smart contracts, bridges). XCM is a messaging format, not a protocol — it defines what messages mean, not how they are transported. Built around a XCVM (Cross-Consensus Virtual Machine) with a register-based instruction set. Enables trustless asset transfers, remote execution, and cross-chain governance across the Polkadot ecosystem and beyond. [a]

name: ERC-7984
description: An Ethereum token standard for confidential fungible tokens. Structurally similar to ERC-20, but balances and transfer amounts are stored on-chain as ciphertext handles — pointers to encrypted values held by a fully homomorphic encryption co-processor — so no amount is publicly readable while transfers remain composable and verifiable. Selective disclosure is possible through view keys, allowing compliance and audit without making balances public. A companion wrapper registry maps existing ERC-20 tokens to their ERC-7984 confidential equivalents, letting any ordinary token gain confidentiality. This is the first entry in this file to use FHE rather than zero-knowledge proofs as its privacy primitive. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Active — reference implementation shipped in OpenZeppelin's Confidential Contracts library with published API documentation and code examples; deployed on Zama's fhEVM. Described as adopted by a growing set of stablecoins, custodians, wallets, compliance tools and exchanges. I could not confirm the formal EIP status field (Draft / Review / Final) from the sources reviewed — verify at eips.ethereum.org before finalising this cell [a][b][c]
owner: Co-authored by OpenZeppelin and Zama, with Inco; the three co-founded the Confidential Token Association, which also involves Stellar, Fhenix and Predicate. Published as an Ethereum ERC through the open EIP process [a][b][c]
governingBody: Ethereum EIP/ERC process | Confidential Token Association (industry consortium co-founded by OpenZeppelin, Zama and Inco, also involving Stellar, Fhenix and Predicate)
country: International — OpenZeppelin, Zama (France) and Inco; the Ethereum EIP process is jurisdiction-independent [a][b]
stack: Solidity — contracts built on OpenZeppelin's Confidential Contracts library, using the Zama fhEVM co-processor for FHE operations on ciphertext handles [a][b]
license: Permissive (MIT) — reference implementation in OpenZeppelin Confidential Contracts; ERC text published openly through the EIP process [a][b]
funding: Corporate / venture — OpenZeppelin and Zama contributed the authoring work; Zama is venture-funded with a token launched February 2026. No separate funding attaches to the standard itself [b][c]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2). Governance & legal control (≈2): published as an open ERC and co-authored by three organizations rather than one, with the Confidential Token Association giving it a multi-stakeholder home including Stellar, Fhenix and Predicate; the reference implementation is MIT-licensed under OpenZeppelin, a widely trusted neutral library maintainer [a][b][c]. Funding & key-org dependency (≈3): the standard is open, but in practice it depends on an FHE co-processor, and Zama is by far the dominant provider — a venture-funded company with its own token. Alternative FHE backends (Inco, Fhenix) exist, which is what keeps this from scoring higher [b][c]. Forking viability (≈2): an open ERC with an MIT reference implementation is trivially forkable at the specification level; the practical constraint is co-processor availability rather than licensing [a][b]. Regulatory / jurisdictional exposure (≈3): confidential transfer of value attracts direct regulatory attention, and the standard's own selective-disclosure design is a response to that pressure [a][c]. Track record: no capture events. Recorded because this entry's privacy guarantee is only as strong as the co-processor operating it — an operational dependency that a pure on-chain standard would not carry [b]

name: Iroh
description: A modular P2P networking stack providing direct, encrypted connections between devices using public key addresses instead of IP addresses. Built by n0, Inc. (Rust; open source; 8K GitHub stars). The core primitive is the Endpoint — a QUIC-based peer identified by a cryptographic key rather than IP address, enabling persistent addressability regardless of network topology. All connections are E2EE over QUIC with no certificate management required. Composable protocol modules include Blobs (resumable, verifiable content-addressed data transfer), Gossip (topic-based broadcast to groups of endpoints), and Documents (realtime multiwriter key-value sync with CRDTs). NAT traversal and relay fallback are built in. Used in production by Delta Chat (real-time sync), Spacedrive (file sync), Nous (distributed AI training), Holochain (DHT transport), and Paycode (offline POS payments). [a]

name: Hypercore
description: Append-only, signed, sparsely-replicated log structure that forms the foundational data primitive of the Holepunch (formerly Hypercore Protocol / dat) ecosystem. Each Hypercore is a single-writer log identified by a public key, with cryptographic verification via Merkle trees enabling secure partial replication between peers. Designed for genuinely peer-to-peer operation with relays used only for hole-punching peer discovery; once peers find each other, all data flows directly between them. [a][b][c]

name: Automerge
description: A CRDT library and accompanying sync protocol for local-first collaborative software. An Automerge document behaves like a JSON object that any number of peers can modify concurrently, offline, and merge without conflict or manual resolution; the library also preserves full change history, allowing version-control-like operations over application data. Version 2.0 rewrote the original JavaScript implementation in Rust, delivering a compact binary document format and substantially better performance, with bindings for JavaScript/WASM, Swift, Python and others. Rich-text support with a ProseMirror binding was added subsequently. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Active — Automerge 2.0 shipped as a Rust rewrite with a stable binary format; rich text support and a fully supported ProseMirror binding added; automerge-repo provides sync and storage adapters. Full-time engineering staffed by Ink & Switch. Widely adopted as the CRDT layer beneath other systems, including DXOS ECHO, and referenced by Iroh, Keyhive, AD4M and NextGraph in this file [a][b][c]
owner: Ink & Switch — the independent industrial research lab provides full-time engineering staff, including lead maintainer Alex Good, Orion Henry, Brooklyn Zelenka and John Mumm. Co-created by Martin Kleppmann (University of Cambridge); the project describes contributors including engineers who co-founded Heroku [b][c]

name: Yjs
description: A high-performance CRDT framework for building collaborative applications, providing shared data types — Y.Map, Y.Array, Y.Text, Y.XmlFragment — that merge concurrent changes automatically. Its distinguishing strengths are speed and ecosystem breadth: bindings exist for most major rich-text and code editors (ProseMirror, TipTap, Quill, CodeMirror, Monaco, Slate), and provider modules supply sync over WebSocket, WebRTC, IndexedDB and other channels. y-protocols defines the awareness and sync message formats. Yjs is the most widely deployed CRDT library in production collaborative software, and underpins several applications in this file. [a][b][c]

name: Mutual Credit Clearing
description: A monetary protocol in which participants extend credit to one another bilaterally through a shared ledger maintained by a third party, with the sum of all account balances structurally constrained to zero. Each transaction simultaneously credits one party and debits another. Prototypes: Sardex (Sardinia, Italy) for institutionalized B2B mutual credit; Local Exchange Trading Systems (LETS) for community-scale implementations. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Closed source (Sardex proprietary platform); open variants exist for LETS. [a]
devStatusNote: Released — Sardex serves over 4,000 SMEs; numerous LETS networks operate globally. [a][b]
owner: Sardex S.p.A. (Sardinia, Italy); LETS networks operated by local communities globally. [a][b]
stack: Proprietary platforms (Sardex); diverse implementations for LETS networks including community-run software. [a]
license: Closed source (Sardex proprietary platform); open variants exist for LETS. [a]
funding: Sardex: private investment, member fees, transaction revenues; LETS: typically volunteer-operated. [a][b]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2): a pattern with both proprietary and open implementations, freely implementable as a grammar. Governance & legal control (≈3): the Sardex platform is proprietary, but open LETS variants exist and the grammar itself is freely implementable [a]. Regulatory / jurisdictional exposure (≈3): Sardex is a regulated commercial mutual-credit operator with financial-regulatory exposure [a]. Funding & key-org dependency (≈3): Sardex runs on private investment and member/transaction fees, while LETS networks are volunteer-operated — a mixed picture [a][c]. Forking viability (≈2): the grammar is open and widely implemented via LETS, even though Sardex's specific platform is proprietary. Track record (≈1): clean, with LETS operating since 1983.

name: Quadratic Funding

name: Civic Process
description: One of four canonical Civic.Social specifications, and the interactive unit of the model. Defines structured, stateful civic processes — voting, participatory budgeting, deliberation — that enable participation between citizens, organizations and institutions. Specifies a process lifecycle (canonical vocabulary plus lifecycle profiles), identity, eligibility and disclosure requirements, integration with the Civic Activity model, and interface contracts for creation, descriptors and actions. A process type is implemented and distributed as a Civic Process Plugin, registered with a host space's process registry; this specification defines the contract a plugin implements, while the companion Civic Plugin Architecture defines how it is packaged, scoped and installed. [b][c]

name: Pubky Protocol
description: An open protocol for per-public-key backends ("homeservers") enabling censorship-resistant web applications with "credible exit" — the freedom to switch homeserver providers without losing data. Identity is an Ed25519 keypair; PKARR (Public Key Addressable Resource Records) publishes DNS-style records to the BitTorrent Mainline DHT for homeserver discovery, while the homeserver itself handles data storage/serving over standard HTTP/REST. Live ecosystem includes pubky.app (social), an Explorer, and demo apps (mapky.app, eventky.app). Structurally comparable to Solid's personal-data-pod-plus-portable-identity model, though homeserver discovery is DHT-based rather than WebFinger/WebID. Formerly called Pubky Core. [a][b]

name: PKARR
description: Public Key Addressable Resource Records — converts an Ed25519 keypair into a self-controlled "domain": DNS-style records (A/AAAA/TXT/CNAME) are signed and published as BEP44 mutable items on the BitTorrent Mainline DHT, resolvable anywhere without registrars or platforms. HTTP-to-DHT relay gateways bridge browser and UDP-restricted clients to the DHT. Built directly on the existing BitTorrent Mainline DHT (P2P Infra) rather than new infrastructure — leverages a 15+ year-old, ~10M+ node network. Serves as the discovery/naming layer under Pubky Protocol's homeserver architecture. [a][b]

name: Buzz
description: A self-hostable chat/workspace platform, built on a Nostr relay, where humans and AI agents share the same rooms — messaging (NIP-01), authenticated presence (NIP-42, Schnorr-signature), git collaboration (NIP-34: patches, repo announcements, status events), and media (Blossom protocol) all ride the same relay. Publicly released by Block, Inc. (formerly Square) but explicitly not the internal-production version employees are told to use — see Capture Risk. Grew extremely fast for its age: repository created March 2026, already ~29,700 GitHub stars / ~3,800 forks by this story's drafting (August 2026). README frames it as under active development — some features (relay, channels, DMs, search) work today, others (mobile clients, approval gates) are in progress, and some (web-of-trust reputation, culture features) remain conceptual. name: Deliberation Interoperability Project
description: A Rust-based common data model and set of platform adaptors for deliberative-democracy tools, from the Metagov research collective (metagov/ontology). Core entities: Person, Statement (roles: Question, Belief, Fact, Evidence, Refutation, Summary, Proposal, Decision), Project, Phase, Reaction, Collection, Event; decision mechanisms include ranked-choice and quadratic voting. Exports to three target formats — RDF/JSON-LD (semantic web/research publication), AT Protocol lexicons (Bluesky/ATproto integration), and JSON Schema (API validation/OpenAPI) — rather than depending on any single transport substrate. Ships platform adaptors for Polis (opinion clustering), HeyForm (forms/polls), and Talk to the City (API-based report generation). Its data-model and adaptor structure appears extracted from CrownShy's Comhairle (github.com/crownshy/comhairle, AGPL-3.0, 1,518 commits) — a real architectural lineage, though Comhairle itself is a conventional AWS/K8s deliberation web platform with no inter-instance protocol of its own and is not itself part of this matrix. Distinct from, and complementary to, this project's existing Decentralized Deliberation Stack (DDS) entry: DDS is a W3C Community Group protocol/interface spec (Plan/Collect/Analyze) built specifically on AT Protocol as a required transport layer, whereas this project defines a transport-agnostic data model with ATProto lexicons as only one of several optional export targets, plus concrete adaptors to existing tools rather than new interfaces. [a]
devStatus: Draft / embryonic — 11 commits on main, no releases, 0 forks, 5 stars, 2 open issues as of this story's drafting (August 2026); early-stage, not yet confirmed adopted by its own listed platform adaptors in production [a]
owner: Metagov research collective (metagov GitHub org) [a]
governingBody: Metagov research collective (no single commercial owner) [a]

funding: Unknown — no funder or sponsor disclosed [a]
captureRiskReasoning: Low (2), but too early to assess with confidence. Governance & legal control (≈2): Metagov is a research-collective/nonprofit-adjacent body, not a single commercial owner. Funding & key-org dependency (≈3): no funder disclosed; embryonic stage means continuity depends on a very small number of contributors. Forking viability (≈2): license intent is stated (MPL-2.0) even though no formal LICENSE file is filed yet — a fixable gap, not a structural lock-in. Regulatory exposure minimal (a data-model/ontology project, no entity/token/ledger). Track record too early to assess (11 commits, no releases). [a]

name: IXO
description: A Spatial Web platform for verifiable impact coordination, giving people, organisations, and AI agents shared state, structure, and rules for coordinating work, financing, verification, and governance. Built around Impact Hub (chain-id ixo-5), a live Cosmos SDK Layer-1 appchain with IBC running custom modules for entities, claims, tokens, bonds, smart accounts, and governance, with W3C-aligned verifiable credentials carrying IXO system identifiers and a decentralized domain registry for digital-twin identifiers. IXO Matrix, a sovereign data/messaging layer on open Matrix Protocol standards, is self-hostable, end-to-end encrypted, and federated across independently-hosted servers, with each room resolvable as a DID on Impact Hub. Agentic oracles — including WISP, which uses Giza zero-knowledge ML for auditable climate impact-claim verification — plus MCP servers extend the platform with AI-driven services. SDKs (@ixo/impactxclient-sdk, @ixo/matrixclient-sdk) and CosmWasm contracts let third parties build against the stack; client apps (IXO Portal, IXO Studio, IXO Mobile, Impacts X, Jambo Wallet) are built on top of it. Deployments include decentralised digital MRV for clean cooking and a Duke-NUS pathogen genomics/infectious-disease intelligence platform (PathGen) previewed December 2025 in Singapore. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Active — mainnet operational since September 2021 genesis, IBC-connected. Latest release v8.0.0 ('Alpha'), an emergency security fix deployed via governance proposal #482 (chain height 17,871,000) in response to vulnerability advisory GHSA-w3rp-4cm2-4wgc: the bonds module is disabled network-wide — all state-changing bonds messages are rejected by the chain, though queries and existing bond state remain readable. [c]
owner: IXO Foundation (non-profit; received 10% of genesis token distribution). Repos are split across two GitHub orgs (ixoworld and ixofoundation), muddying single-owner attribution — ixofoundation hosts the flagship ixo-blockchain repo and is the org referenced throughout this entry. [a][b][d]
governingBody: IXO Foundation (non-profit steward/registrant) | On-chain governance module (Cosmos governance proposals; IXO-token holders vote — the 40% Community Pool specifically requires such a proposal to disburse, with a dedicated DAO intended to eventually take over ecosystem-investment decisions, not yet established). [b][c][d]
country: Switzerland (Zug) — per two independent third-party organisation profiles (Solar Impulse World Alliance, Blockchain for Social Impact); not independently confirmed via IXO's own primary site. [f][g]
stack: Go — Cosmos SDK Layer-1 appchain (chain-id ixo-5) with CometBFT/Tendermint consensus and IBC; CosmWasm for smart contracts; Matrix Protocol (via IXO Matrix, a separately-federated messaging layer); TypeScript SDKs (@ixo/impactxclient-sdk, @ixo/matrixclient-sdk). [a][b][c]
license: Apache-2.0 (org-wide default across github.com/ixofoundation, confirmed independently on the ixo-blockchain repo; one named exception — local-ixo uses MIT). [b]
funding: Foundation-backed (IXO Non-profit Foundation, 10% of genesis token distribution) plus a native IXO token — 100M minted at September 2021 genesis, 40% (40M) held in an authorised-but-unissued Community Pool requiring Network Governance Proposals to disburse, intended for eventual DAO-governed ecosystem investment. [b][d]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (≈3): Apache-2.0 code, but IXO Foundation (Zug, Switzerland) is the practical steward, and though a Cosmos governance module exists, the 40% Community Pool requires governance-proposal disbursement rather than free availability — meaningful token-holder-gated control that hasn't yet transitioned to a dedicated DAO; repos split across two GitHub orgs is a minor governance-clarity signal. [a][b][d] Funding & key-org dependency (≈3): foundation-backed with a native token; ecosystem-investment activity is tied to Community Pool governance-proposal activity that hasn't yet materialized into a DAO. [d] Forking viability (≈3): Apache-2.0 Cosmos SDK code is straightforwardly forkable as software, but chain state, IXO system identifiers, and token economics are bound to the specific ixo-5 network — a fork would not carry existing identifiers or claims. [b][c] Regulatory exposure (≈4): a transferable native token used within a financing/governance model attracts securities/financial-services attention typical of Cosmos appchains with native tokens. Track record: a real, disclosed security incident — the bonds module was disabled network-wide in v8.0.0 as an emergency response to a published vulnerability advisory (GHSA-w3rp-4cm2-4wgc), handled transparently via a public governance proposal and changelog rather than silently — recorded factually as both a genuine incident and evidence the security-response process functions. [c]

name: Bitcoin
description: The original peer-to-peer electronic cash protocol — a decentralized, trust-minimized ledger secured by Proof-of-Work mining, with no central issuer or validator set. Bitcoin Core is the reference implementation; independent implementations (btcd, bcoin, libbitcoin) exist and must conform to the same consensus rules. Protocol changes go through the informal Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) process — rough consensus among node operators, miners, and developers, not a formal vote. [a]
devStatus: Active — continuous mainnet operation since 2009, ongoing BIP-driven development [a]
owner: No single owner — an open-source project with a large, distributed contributor base.
governingBody: None (informal rough consensus via the BIP process; no foundation or company holds authority over consensus rules). [a]
stack: C++ (Bitcoin Core); independent implementations exist in Go (btcd), JavaScript (bcoin), and C++ (libbitcoin) conforming to the same protocol.
license: MIT [a]
funding: No formal funding entity; Bitcoin Core development is funded via a mix of individual, company (e.g. exchanges, mining firms), and grant-based sponsorship of individual contributors, not a treasury.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2). Governance & legal control (~1): no company or foundation controls consensus rules; the BIP process is genuinely open, rough-consensus-based. Funding & key-org dependency (~2): development funding is diversified across many independent contributors and sponsoring organizations, no single point of failure. Forking viability (~1): MIT-licensed, multiple independent implementations already exist and interoperate. Regulatory exposure (~3): BTC itself is a widely-regulated asset in many jurisdictions, though the protocol itself has no legal entity to target. Track record: no capture events in 15+ years of operation. [a]

name: Ethereum
description: A programmable, smart-contract-capable blockchain protocol. Unlike Bitcoin's narrow scripting, Ethereum runs a Turing-complete virtual machine (the EVM), enabling arbitrary decentralized applications. Multiple independent client implementations exist (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Reth, Erigon) that must conform to the same consensus rules, developed through the Ethereum Improvement Proposal (EIP) process — informal rough consensus among client teams, researchers, and the Ethereum Foundation, not a foundation directive. Transitioned from Proof-of-Work to Proof-of-Stake in September 2022 ("the Merge"). [a]
devStatus: Active — continuous mainnet operation since 2015, ongoing EIP-driven development [a]
owner: No single owner — multiple independent client teams (Geth/EF, Nethermind, Besu/Hyperledger, Reth/Paradigm, Erigon) plus a broad open-source contributor base.
governingBody: None with unilateral authority — the EIP process is community rough-consensus; the Ethereum Foundation (Swiss nonprofit) funds research/development but does not control protocol changes unilaterally.
country: N/A (globally distributed; Ethereum Foundation is Swiss-registered but doesn't control the protocol)
stack: Multi-client — Go (Geth), C# (Nethermind), Java (Besu), Rust (Reth), Go (Erigon); all implement the same EVM/consensus spec.
license: Multi-client, no single license — reference client (Geth) is LGPL-3.0/GPL-3.0 dual; other major clients use their own licenses (Besu Apache-2.0, Nethermind LGPL-3.0, Reth MIT/Apache-2.0 dual). [b]
funding: Ethereum Foundation grants/research funding; individual client teams also receive separate funding (e.g. Reth from Paradigm, a VC firm) — funding is genuinely distributed across multiple independent organizations, not centralized.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (~3): genuinely multi-client and rough-consensus-governed, but the Ethereum Foundation's research/funding role and its influence over the EIP roadmap give it outsized (if non-binding) influence relative to Bitcoin's more diffuse model. Funding & key-org dependency (~3): funding is distributed across EF plus independent client-team backers (e.g. Paradigm for Reth), reducing single-point dependency, but EF remains the most influential funder. Forking viability (~2): multiple independent, actively-maintained client implementations already exist under permissive licenses. Regulatory exposure (~4): ETH is a widely-scrutinized asset (SEC attention, MiCA classification debates in the EU). Track record: no consensus-level capture events, though contentious hard forks (the 2016 DAO fork) show the community has split before under pressure. [a][b]

name: IBC (Inter-Blockchain Communication Protocol)
description: An open protocol for secure, trust-minimized communication between independent blockchains ("interchain") — packet-based message passing with light-client verification, not a trusted bridge/relay. Defined as a formal spec (ICS — Interchain Standards) in the cosmos/ibc repository, with ibc-go and ibc-rs as reference implementations for Cosmos SDK and Rust-based chains respectively. Maintained by a "Protocol team," though individual standards have alternate maintainers (e.g. ICS-32 is maintained by Strangelove Ventures, not the core team) — a genuinely distributed governance model for the spec itself. [a]
devStatus: Active — mainnet-ready since 2021, live in production connecting 100+ chains [a]
owner: No single owner — a "Protocol team" maintains the core spec, with individual ICS standards sometimes maintained by other organizations (Strangelove Ventures, Cosmos Hub team).
governingBody: Community-governed spec repository; no single company or foundation controls it, though the Interchain Foundation has historically funded core development.
stack: Protocol-agnostic spec; primary implementations in Go (ibc-go, for Cosmos SDK chains) and Rust (ibc-rs).
license: Apache-2.0 [a]
funding: Historically Interchain Foundation-funded (grants to core maintainers); individual ICS standards may have other funders (e.g. Strangelove Ventures self-funds its own maintained standards).
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2). Governance & legal control (~2): the spec repo is genuinely multi-maintainer with distinct standards owned by different organizations — no single entity controls the whole spec. Funding & key-org dependency (~2): historically ICF-funded but individual standards' maintainers are independently funded/self-funded. Forking viability (~1): Apache-2.0, spec-based, multiple independent implementations already exist. Regulatory exposure (~1): a communication protocol, not a token or financial instrument itself. Track record: no capture events; the multi-maintainer structure is itself evidence against concentration. [a]

name: Cardano

The cardano-node repository is now maintained under IntersectMBO (renamed from the original Input Output HK organization in 2023). [a]

captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (~2-3): genuinely live on-chain governance (DReps, Constitutional Committee, SPOs) is a real, binding decentralization mechanism, unusually mature for this batch — but the three founding entities (IntersectMBO, Cardano Foundation, Emurgo) retain outsized historical influence and technical stewardship. Funding & key-org dependency (~3): a real on-chain Treasury reduces dependency on any single funder, but the founding trio still drives most core development. Forking viability (~2): Apache-2.0, open-source. Regulatory exposure (~4): ADA has drawn direct SEC scrutiny (named in enforcement actions against exchanges). Track record: no capture events; the Voltaire transition itself is evidence of a genuine decentralization trajectory. [a]

entityAttributes.developmentTools: SDK/tooling for launching rollups and app-chains against the Celestia DA layer (positioned as the core product per current homepage framing).

entityAttributes.interoperability: IBC-compatible (inherits from its Cosmos SDK base), plus its core purpose is serving as a shared DA layer other chains depend on.

name: Monero
description: A privacy-first cryptocurrency protocol using ring signatures, stealth addresses, and RingCT to obscure sender, receiver, and transaction amount by default (not opt-in privacy). RandomX (a CPU-optimized Proof-of-Work algorithm, adopted 2019) is the current consensus mechanism, chosen specifically to resist ASIC mining centralization. No foundation or company controls it — development is fully community/donation-funded via the Monero Community Crowdfunding System (CCS). [a]
devStatus: Active — continuous mainnet operation since 2014, ongoing donation-funded development [a]
owner: No single owner — an open-source project with a distributed contributor base (the Monero Core Team acts as a coordinating/signing group, not an owning entity).
governingBody: None (community-governed; CCS funds specific proposals, no central authority).
license: BSD-3-Clause
funding: Monero Community Crowdfunding System (CCS) — donation-based, proposal-by-proposal funding, no venture capital or foundation treasury.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Minimal (1). Governance & legal control (~1): no foundation, no company, no single controlling entity of any kind — one of the most genuinely decentralized governance models in this entire batch. Funding & key-org dependency (~2): CCS donation funding is proposal-by-proposal and broadly sourced, though the Core Team's coordinating role is itself a soft dependency. Forking viability (~1): BSD-3-Clause, fully open. Regulatory exposure (~4): privacy coins specifically (Monero named directly) have faced exchange delistings and regulatory pressure in multiple jurisdictions precisely because of the privacy-by-default design. Track record: no capture events; the project's entire history is one of resisting centralizing pressure (e.g. the deliberate RandomX PoW change specifically to defeat ASIC centralization). [a]

references.note: "Private, decentralized cryptocurrency that keeps your finances confidential and secure"; confirms community-driven development supported by volunteers and the Community Crowdfunding System (CCS)

name: Zcash
description: "Encrypted electronic cash" — the first cryptocurrency to implement zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs, via the Zerocash protocol) for optional fully-shielded, privacy-preserving transactions, built on a Bitcoin-derived codebase. Governance is genuinely multi-stakeholder: Electric Coin Company (the original for-profit developer), the Zcash Foundation (non-profit), and Zcash Community Grants (a community-elected funding body) all play distinct roles, trending toward more community control since 2020. [a]
devStatus: Active — mainnet since 2016, ongoing multi-stakeholder development [a] Update (July 2026): the reference node zcashd reached end of life on 18 July 2026 (its repository was archived on 19 July) and is succeeded by the Zebra and Zakura node implementations and the Zallet wallet; the protocol and network continue [c]
owner: Electric Coin Company (original developer, for-profit) — but not the sole steward; see Governing Body.
governingBody: Multi-stakeholder — Electric Coin Company (core dev), Zcash Foundation (non-profit, ecosystem/protocol stewardship), Zcash Community Grants (community-elected dev-fund allocation body). No single entity holds unilateral authority.
stack: C++ (zcash/zcash, Bitcoin-derived codebase).
license: MIT — confirmed via the repo's COPYING file. One narrow exception worth noting: the bundled Oracle Berkeley DB 6.2.x dependency is separately AGPL-licensed. [b]
funding: Multi-source — Electric Coin Company's own revenue/investment, Zcash Foundation grants, and the on-chain "dev fund" allocated in part via Zcash Community Grants' community-elected process.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (~3): genuinely multi-stakeholder (ECC + Foundation + Community Grants), a real check-and-balance structure, but ECC's founding/technical role still gives it outsized practical influence relative to a fully community-elected model. Funding & key-org dependency (~3): diversified across the three entities, reducing single-point risk somewhat. Forking viability (~2): MIT, genuinely open (with the noted narrow AGPL dependency exception). Regulatory exposure (~4): like Monero, a privacy-coin specifically named in exchange delistings and MiCA-adjacent regulatory discussions. Track record: no capture events; the multi-stakeholder evolution since 2020 (moving away from a purely ECC-controlled model) is itself evidence of a genuine decentralization trajectory. [a]

references.note: "encrypted electronic cash," "the first cryptocurrency to develop zero-knowledge encryption for private peer-to-peer payments"; names Electric Coin Co., Zcash Foundation, and Zcash Community Grants as the ecosystem's governance entities
MIT License confirmed, with a noted AGPL exception for the bundled Berkeley DB 6.2.x dependency
zcashd README: 'zcashd has reached its End of Life', final halt on 18 July 2026 at block height 3417100, succeeded by Zebra, Zakura and Zallet (read 2026-11-12)

name: XRP Ledger
description: A decentralized public ledger using its own Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus algorithm (distinct from both PoW and PoS — validators vote on transaction ordering via the XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol), operational since 2012. Naming precision: this entity is the XRP Ledger (the protocol/network), not "Ripple" — Ripple is a company that "acts as a steward for the technology" (confirmed directly from the rippled repo's own README) but does not own or unilaterally control the ledger; a team of developers "at Ripple & other organizations" maintain the reference software. [a]
devStatus: Active — "10+ years of error-free, uninterrupted performance" per xrpl.org's own claim, ongoing development [a][b]
owner: No single owner — rippled (the reference server software) is developed by "a team of full-time developers at Ripple & other organizations."
governingBody: Validator-based amendment voting (on-chain governance mechanism where a supermajority of trusted validators must approve protocol changes) — but Ripple the company remains highly influential as the largest single contributor to core development and a major validator-list curator.
country: N/A (Ripple, the primary corporate steward, is US-based; the ledger itself has no jurisdiction)
stack: C++ (rippled, the reference server implementation).
license: ISC [a]
funding: Ripple (the company) funds the majority of core rippled development; other organizations also contribute.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (~4): a formal validator-amendment-voting mechanism is real and on-chain, but Ripple's role as both the largest development contributor and an influential voice in the recommended validator list gives it dominant practical control — a company being the dominant steward of a network isn't the same thing as genuine community stewardship, so `single-company` is the more honest label than `community` despite the on-chain voting mechanism existing. Funding & key-org dependency (~4): Ripple funds the majority of core development; the ledger's continued development is materially dependent on one company's continued investment. Forking viability (~2): ISC-licensed, genuinely open-source. Regulatory exposure (~4): XRP was the subject of a prolonged, high-profile SEC enforcement action against Ripple specifically (resolved 2023-2024) — among the most direct regulatory-exposure histories of any entity in this batch. Track record: no on-chain capture events, but the SEC litigation is a material historical event worth naming directly. [a]

references.note: ISC license confirmed; README: "a decentralized cryptographic ledger powered by a network of peer-to-peer nodes" using "a novel Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus algorithm"; explicitly states "Ripple acts as a steward for the technology" and "a team of full-time developers at Ripple & other organizations maintain and continually improve the XRP Ledger's underlying software"
"The Blockchain Built for Business," "10+ years of error-free, uninterrupted performance," self-described as maintained by "a global community of businesses and developers"

name: SpiritDAO Community App
description: A token-gated, multi-community coordination platform built and stewarded by SpiritDAO, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Any group can create a self-governing Pod with its own treasury, roles, governance, forum, chat, video, events, bounties, marketplace, and a per-pod AI agent, running on the Base L2 blockchain with open enrollment. [a]
devStatus: Active, in production, open enrollment. Version 0.35.x, in active development. Documented planned work not yet shipped: cross-community Tenure recognition weights (federation across communities) and governance staking of $SELF (a contract lock seam exists but is not yet wired up). [a]
owner: SpiritDAO, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit (EIN 99-1308806) [a]
governingBody: SpiritDAO nonprofit maintains the codebase and controls application releases and contract deployments; DAO-wide constitutional changes are decided by on-chain votes of Advocate credential holders, executed via timelock; individual Pods govern their own treasuries and operations [a]
stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 18, TypeScript, Progressive Web App; Base L2 for on-chain state (viem/wagmi/OnchainKit, Hats Protocol roles); Coinbase CDP embedded wallets (ERC-4337) with Coinbase Paymaster for gasless writes; Supabase (Postgres, Row-Level Security, Realtime) for application data/auth; Stripe for fiat donations; LiveKit (self-hosted) plus WebRTC for video; Anthropic Claude + OpenAI embeddings + Pinecone for AI/RAG (Kairos, Sensemaker); hosted on Vercel (app) and Cloudflare Pages (site/docs) [a]
license: MIT (per the repository LICENSE); the source repository is not currently public [a]
funding: Donations (tax-deductible, via Stripe); the nonprofit states it is sustained by donations, not subscriptions, venture capital, or advertising [a]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (≈3-4): the nonprofit directly controls the software's own release process and contract deployments — on-chain voting governs constitutional/pod matters, not the app's own releases, a real distinction from projects where chain governance gates the software itself (contrast IXO) [a]. Funding & key-org dependency (≈3): single 501(c)(3) nonprofit, donation-funded, no VC — meaningful reliance on one organization's continued operation, though its nonprofit/mission framing and published governance research suggest some accountability pressure beyond a typical single-vendor risk [a]. Forking viability (≈4, the weakest dimension): MIT-licensed in principle, but the source repository is not currently public — a real, present-tense capture-risk signal distinct from a merely-permissive license; nothing can actually be forked today regardless of the stated license terms [a]. Regulatory exposure (≈3-4): $SYSTEM is a capital-backed, transferable ERC-20 redeemable back to fiat, backed roughly 1:1 by USD held by the nonprofit and minted from donations — a redeemable, donation-backed instrument of this shape plausibly attracts securities/money-transmission scrutiny [a]. Track record: the spec itself publishes an unusually candid dependency-centralization table (about a dozen providers rated for portability if lost) — only Coinbase CDP embedded wallets is rated Low portability (genuinely hard to replace: 'new wallet infrastructure and re-linking members'); Coinbase Paymaster, Supabase, Anthropic, OpenAI, Pinecone and Stripe are Medium; Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, self-hosted LiveKit and Upstash Redis are High (replaceable, though losing Vercel takes the app offline until redeployed). This self-disclosed centralization audit is itself a positive transparency signal, even though the aggregate dependency footprint is real and material [a].

Mission framing (the "Eight Dignities"), nonprofit status, and the "Congregant, Not Citizen" research paper on constitutional design for AI members

name: GRC-20
description: GRC-20 is an open data standard for structuring and connecting knowledge on The Graph — entities, attributes, and values grouped into governed "Spaces," with relations as graph edges and Protobuf-encoded, content-addressed records. Authored by Yaniv Tal and Byron Guina (Draft v0.1.0, CC0), it aims to "do for knowledge what ERC-20 did for fungible tokens": a common, composable schema any web3 application can read and write against, rather than each project inventing its own. Geo Genesis is the standard's flagship application; Hypergraph is its local-first SDK/framework. [a][b]
devStatus: Draft, v0.1.0 (created 2024-11-21) — the specification itself has not moved past Draft status on the GIP track. In practice the standard is not merely theoretical: it is the data model behind the live (testnet) Geo Genesis app and the actively-maintained Hypergraph SDK (Developer Preview, MIT-licensed, TypeScript). No query-language or RDF-interop layer is specified in the GIP itself — the document explicitly rejects RDF compatibility as unsuited to web3 (see Semantic Web Compatibility). [a][c][d]
owner: The Graph Improvement Proposals process (graphprotocol/graph-improvement-proposals repo); authored by Yaniv Tal and Byron Guina. No single corporate owner — a public, CC0-licensed specification. [a]
governingBody: The Graph's Graph Improvement Proposals (GIP) process and repository — a public review track, not a neutral standards body (contrast W3C/IETF). No corporate owner of the specification itself. [a]
country: Not specified — GRC-20 is a specification document, not an organization with a registered location. [a]
stack: Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) for encoding; no single reference-implementation language — the specification is implementation-neutral, though its flagship implementations (Geo Genesis, Hypergraph) are TypeScript/JavaScript. [a][c]
license: CC0 (public domain) — stated directly in the GIP header. [a]
funding: Not itself funded — a public specification. Its stewarding ecosystem (The Graph) is VC-backed with a live token (GRT); see Capture Risk Assessment. [a][b]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (≈3): GRC-20 itself is a CC0 public-domain specification with no corporate owner, authored under The Graph's own GIP process — genuinely open at the standard level. But its only current implementations (Geo Genesis, Hypergraph) are steered respectively by one company (Geo Browser, PB LLC) and The Graph's own org, and the standard positions itself as a successor to RDF/semantic-web approaches rather than building on a neutral multi-stakeholder body like W3C. [a][c][d] Funding & key-org dependency (≈3-4): the standard's practical adoption depends on The Graph ecosystem's continued backing — The Graph is a VC-backed protocol with a live traded token (GRT) and has raised funding from investors including Coinbase Ventures, Multicoin Capital, and Digital Currency Group across multiple rounds since 2019. [b] Forking viability (≈2): CC0 licensing and content-addressed (IPFS-referenceable), Protobuf-encoded data give genuinely strong fork/reuse resilience — any application can implement GRC-20 independent of Geo or The Graph, and the spec is explicitly designed to be usable by "any application." [a] Regulatory exposure (≈2-3): the standard itself carries no token or payment layer; exposure would come only through what's built on it, not the schema itself. Not captureRisk 4-5: this is an open, CC0 specification, not an extractive platform — the moderate score reflects ecosystem-dependency risk, not the standard's own openness. [a][b]

entityAttributes.origins: Knowledge Base / Ecosystem-SDK — created to give web3 applications a common, interoperable schema for structured knowledge, explicitly framed as filling a gap RDF/the semantic web left unaddressed for a decentralized, non-server-dependent web. [a]
entityAttributes.database: No native database — GRC-20 is a data model/encoding specification, not a storage system. Implementations choose their own storage (e.g. Geo Genesis anchors public Spaces on-chain with IPFS content-addressing; Hypergraph is local-first with P2P sync). [a][c]
entityAttributes.queryLanguage: Not specified in the GIP — the specification defines the data model and encoding only, not a query interface. The Graph's own GraphQL/subgraph layer is the likely query surface for GRC-20 data in practice, but this is not confirmed as GRC-20-native in the sources reviewed. [a]

name: Geo Genesis
description: The end-user application for GRC-20 — a knowledge-graph browser where communities create "Spaces" (topic domains), add entities/relations as claims, and govern their own content through Editor/Member voting. Each Space is deployed as its own on-chain Aragon OSx DAO, with data stored on IPFS and indexed via The Graph. Built and released by Geo Browser, PB LLC; still in beta on Geo's own testnet, with write access opening to users in staged batches. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Beta, testnet-only. The project's own MAINNET_CUTOVER_PLAN.md (updated 2026-07-23) states plainly: "We are staying on testnet for now" — current chain id 55516 (GeoTestnetConfig), a planned mainnet chain id (80451) not yet live, no cutover date set. The README describes "opening write permissions to users in small batches" as ongoing work. Each Space is a real on-chain Aragon OSx DAO (confirmed via Aragon's own writeup), not merely a roadmap description — genuine smart-contract governance, just not yet on a permanent mainnet. [c][d][e]
owner: Geo Browser, PB LLC (2025 copyright notice on geobrowser.io) [a]
governingBody: Geo Browser, PB LLC controls the application's own releases, feature rollout pace (e.g. staged write-permission batching), and the mainnet-cutover timeline; each Space's on-chain Aragon OSx DAO governs that Space's knowledge content (Editor/Member voting), not the platform's software. [a][c][d]
country: Not confirmed in the sources reviewed — no registered address or jurisdiction found for Geo Browser, PB LLC. [a][b]
stack: TypeScript/JavaScript monorepo (Bun + Turbo, Docker); Next.js-style web app (apps/web); ZeroDev EIP-7702 smart-wallet stack (Privy EOA-keyed); Aragon OSx contracts per Space; @geoprotocol/geo-sdk. [b][d]
license: Not open source in practice — no LICENSE file exists in the geobrowser/geogenesis repository root (confirmed via GitHub's license-detection API, which returns no result, and a directory listing). The repo's own package.json declares "license": "ISC", but with no LICENSE file to substantiate it, this is a declared-but-textually-unbacked claim, not a verifiable open license — default copyright applies. Distinct from GRC-20's own CC0 status. [b]
funding: Not confirmed in the sources reviewed — no disclosed funding round or backer specific to Geo Browser, PB LLC. The project is closely tied to The Graph (shared founder Yaniv Tal, shared indexing infrastructure), and The Graph itself is VC-backed with a live traded token (GRT) — relevant context, not a direct funding fact about Geo Browser, PB LLC itself. [c][f]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3). Governance & legal control (≈3): on-chain Space governance (Editors vote, Members contribute) is a real decentralization signal — each Space is a genuine on-chain Aragon OSx DAO, not just a policy promise — but the application itself (releases, feature rollout, the mainnet-cutover timeline) is controlled by one company, Geo Browser, PB LLC. [a][c][d] Funding & key-org dependency (≈3-4): not itself confirmed as separately funded; tightly coupled to The Graph (shared founder Yaniv Tal, shared indexing infrastructure), and The Graph is VC-backed with a live traded token (GRT), having raised funding from Coinbase Ventures, Multicoin Capital, and Digital Currency Group among others since 2019. [b][f] Forking viability (≈3-4): the underlying GRC-20 data model is CC0 and portable, but the application's own code carries no verifiable open license — no LICENSE file exists in the repo despite a package.json license claim — so the app itself is not confirmed forkable today regardless of the data's own openness. [b] Regulatory exposure (≈2-3): no distinct token confirmed for Geo/Spaces (see Economic Flows); a knowledge-graph application carries less direct securities exposure than a monetary protocol. Not captureRisk 4-5: this is an early-stage open-knowledge project with real (if young) on-chain governance, not an extractive attention platform. [a][c]
