name: Trustgraphs
description: A platform of zero-knowledge-proven graphs. Community members publicly vouch for one another (recorded as Ethereum Attestation Service attestations); a Trust-Aware PageRank over that graph, with trust flowing from a curated seed set so Sybil rings stay isolated, produces reputation scores. Anyone can compute the scores and prove the computation with an SP1 zero-knowledge proof; an Ethereum mainnet contract verifies the proof and commits the account-to-score Merkle root, which governance weight, reward distribution and Safe owner sets can consume. The proof shows the program ran correctly over the inputs it was designed to authenticate; it does not decide whether the source data is meaningful or whether the community chose good rules. Eight programs are documented (trust graph, weighted prior, contributions, Hypercerts, Nostr workspace, score composition, signer sync, off-chain EAS); only three are self-service. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Alpha. The README calls it highly experimental; the site FAQ says it is still pre-production and not audited by an outside firm; the site header badge reads alpha. Against that, the deployment record marks the Ethereum mainnet instance stage: production. Only one network exists (a research/culture network with 13 scored accounts). Roadmap labels: on-chain EAS current; off-chain EAS, Nostr and AT Protocol pilot; private graphs research. v0.1.5 released 2026-09-14; last push 2026-10-21. [a][c][e][f]
owner: Ainima ("Collective Co-evolutionary Intelligence"; GitHub organisation AInima-Collective) [a][d]
governingBody: Ainima operates the platform and its curated networks. Mainnet admin roles (instance registry, proving vault, subnetwork registry) sit with an admin Safe whose signers are not published in the cited sources. Each network is governed by its own controller; the standard creation wizard makes a DAO Safe the network admin. [a][d][i]
stack: TypeScript; Rust cores; Solidity contracts on Ethereum mainnet; SP1 zkVM guest programs (Groth16 proofs); EAS; IPFS; Safe; Postgres-backed indexer [a][h]
license: MIT (LICENSE file in the repository; its copyright line reads "Copyright 2025 Layer Labs"); https://github.com/AInima-Collective/trustgraphs [a][g]
funding: Sponsored by Gitcoin (per the README acknowledgements); no other funding stated. [a]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3): an MIT-licensed, permissionlessly usable platform whose practical control is concentrated in one small organisation. Governance & Legal Control: Ainima operates the platform and curates the networks; mainnet admin roles are held by a Safe whose signers are not published, and the sole network's protected settings sit under a Safe with threshold 1 and a single plain-wallet owner [i][j]; the licence copyright line names another party without explanation [g]. Regulatory: no jurisdiction stated; reputation scoring is not a regulated service on its face. Funding & Key-org Dependency: Gitcoin is the only named sponsor [a]; Ainima-curated networks are proven at its expense [c]; two developers wrote nearly all commits [a]. Forking Viability: MIT, deterministic public programs, no standard upgradeable-proxy pattern seen on the contracts checked [a][h][j]; proving hardware or the Succinct prover network is needed [a]. Track Record: short history, no capture events on record. The proof establishes correct computation over authenticated inputs, not that the data or rules are good [b]. No outside audit [c]. Seed sets are chosen by each network's controller, a social capture surface at the network layer.

name: Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS)
description: Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS): an open-source, permissionless, tokenless infrastructure public good for making attestations onchain or offchain. Two smart contracts: a schema registry and an attester; schemas can be registered for any use case and may carry a resolver contract for onchain verification or payments. An attestation is a digital signature on structured data. It makes no assumption about schema structure or use, and is not an identity provider. [a][b]
devStatus: Active. Deployed to the Ethereum mainnet and about a dozen other EVM networks (Optimism, Base, Arbitrum One and Nova, Polygon, Scroll, zkSync, Celo, Blast, Linea); contract versions on the deployments page range from 0.26 to 1.3.0. Contracts repository last pushed 2026-07-16, SDK 2026-08-27. The test-coverage report on the docs site is dated 2023-10-31 (100%). [a][c][d]
owner: Not stated by the project (GitHub organisation "Ethereum Attestation Service"; no legal entity named in the cited sources). [a][c]
governingBody: None stated. The documentation describes the project as an open-source public good built by the community for the community; no governing body, legal entity or decision process is documented in the cited sources. [a][b]
stack: Solidity / EVM (EAS and SchemaRegistry contracts, resolver contracts, EIP-712 proxy, indexer contract); TypeScript SDK [c][d]
license: MIT; https://github.com/ethereum-attestation-service/eas-contracts [c]
funding: Not stated by the project in the cited sources. The contracts repository carries a funding.json pointing to an Optimism retroactive-funding project entry; the docs describe grants, retroactive funding and donations as ways such public goods are funded. [b][c]
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2), provisional — based on public documentation only: an MIT-licensed attestation registry with no owner function and no standard upgradeable-proxy pattern on the Ethereum deployment [e]. Governance & Legal Control: no governing body or legal entity is documented [a][b]. Regulatory: no entity or country stated. name: Hypercerts
description: An open protocol for tracking, evaluating and funding impact work. Impact claims ("hypercerts") and their parts — contributions, rights, work scope, evidence attachments, measurements, evaluations, acknowledgements, collections and a governed tag vocabulary — are defined as AT Protocol Lexicon schemas and live as records in repositories their authors control, not on a blockchain. Anyone can review, vouch for, or back a claim. [a][b]
devStatus: Alpha / in development. Lexicons at v1.6.0, API v0.2.0; the docs mark several components as under development and the earlier SDK as deprecated as of early 2026. Lexicon repository last pushed 2026-10-27 (745 commits). [a][b]

license: MIT (lexicons); Apache-2.0 (relay); https://github.com/hypercerts-org/hypercerts-lexicon [b]
funding: Supporters named in the organisation profile: Protocol Labs, Ma Earth, GainForest, Optimism, Octant, Gitcoin, Silvi, Regen Foundation, Funding the Commons (the project states that support does not imply endorsement) [a]

Governance & Legal Control: a single foundation stewards the lexicons and relay; its governance process and jurisdiction are not documented in the cited sources. Regulatory: jurisdiction not stated. Funding & Key-org Dependency: nine or more named supporters, none dominant [a]. Forking Viability: MIT / Apache-2.0, plain schema JSON, portable records [b]. name: The Weave
description: An approach to group software built from small, linkable units of social context, with the Weave Interaction Pattern (WIP) as its open standard for creating, searching, linking and organising them across groupware tools. The WIP is a set of conventions on top of Holochain: assets and their identifiers and semantic trees, Weave Asset Locators (a Holochain resource locator plus an asset identifier) that let one tool point at another's data, renderer types a tool must provide, search and discovery functions, notification definitions, and shared group services. It is not a formal specification today: the project says it is deliberately not writing a hard spec yet, and the developer documentation is marked as under construction. Moss is its reference runtime. [a][b][c]
devStatus: WIP. The pattern is still emerging from use: no formal or draft specification of the WIP or of Weave Asset Locators is published, and the developer docs are marked "under construction". The reference runtime, Moss, is described by its site as in group-onboarding beta (v0.15.8 downloads for macOS, Linux and Windows). [a][b][e]
owner: Lightningrod Labs and Holochain (as the project's site states: "brought to you by") [a]
governingBody: Lightningrod Labs and Holochain; no governance process documented. Default Tool curation list maintained by Lightningrod Labs [a][d]
stack: Holochain; TypeScript (@theweave/api WeaveClient); Moss as the reference frame (Rust / TypeScript) [b][c][f]
license: Software: Moss (the reference runtime) is CAL-1.0 per its README; licences for the WIP documentation's APIs and tooling are not stated in the cited sources. Website content: CC BY-SA 4.0. https://github.com/lightningrodlabs/moss [a][f]
funding: Not stated by the project.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Low (2), provisional — based on public documentation only: an open pattern stewarded by two organisations, with Moss, the only reference runtime, under a copyleft licence. Governance & Legal Control (3): Lightningrod Labs and Holochain steward it with no documented governance or decision process [a]; Lightningrod Labs maintains the default Tool curation list and merges additions by pull request [d]; Moss's copyright is held by a company [e][f] and the licences covering the WIP's APIs are not stated, so who could relicense those is unclear. Regulatory (2): no jurisdiction stated. Funding & Key-org Dependency (3): funding is not stated; the work is concentrated in the two stewarding organisations [a]. Forking Viability (3): Moss is open source, but with no written spec a third party would have to re-derive the pattern from the docs and from Moss's behaviour [a][b], and it depends on Holochain. Track Record (1): no capture-favoring decisions found; the project renamed from "We" to The Weave [f], which is not one.

name: Membership Card Protocol
description: A protocol for community-issued membership credentials ("cards"). A community writes a card policy: who may issue, what a card attests, how it may be updated or revoked. An issuer offers a card, the holder countersigns with a key they generate themselves, and a "press" holding an on-chain authorization checks the policy and registers the card. The card's current state is a pointer in a registry contract on Arbitrum One and its history is an append-only encrypted log on IPFS. Cards are private by default, designed not to be linkable to each other, can receive encrypted messages, and are verified by walking the chain of cards back to a trusted root. The README calls the protocol "fully decentralized", while the assurances page calls it "federated": presses, relays, wallet services and notaries are independently operated roles authorized by cards rather than a central administrator, and a press can lose its authorization [b][c]. Today it is a small project of one organisation with one contributor, a draft specification and no real-world communities yet. [a][c][d]
devStatus: Alpha. The specification (v0.4, 2026-07-04) is a draft marked "In Review" [d]. Three contracts are deployed to Arbitrum One mainnet (2026-08-20 per the deployment record; contract code present at all three addresses when checked 2026-10-29) [f]. Against that, the site says the protocol is in development, that a partial security review is done but a thorough review and third-party auditing are not, and that partnerships with real-world communities and the frontend app are not done [a]; the assurances page calls its guarantees design targets that are not verified today [b]. No releases or tags; one contributor [c].
owner: Relationality Lab [a][g]
governingBody: Relationality Lab (author and operator today). Designed governance, per the project: RootPolicyBody (4-of-5; policy registration and logic upgrades), PressRegistryBody (4-of-5; press authorization and revocation) and DnsGovernanceBody (M-of-N, bootstrapped 1-of-1; the mcard:// namespace), all with on-chain quorum keys; the materials do not state that any body has convened [e]
stack: TypeScript services and SDKs; Rust contracts on Arbitrum Stylus; Arbitrum One; IPFS; ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204) and secp256r1 signatures; ML-KEM message encryption; AES-256-GCM [c][d][f]
license: No licence file was found in the repository (checked 2026-10-29); the project describes itself as free to use and open source [a]. https://github.com/davidgljay/membership_card_protocol [c]
funding: Not stated by the project.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3), provisional, from public documentation only. Governance & Legal Control (4): one organisation writes and operates the protocol today; its governance design is three on-chain bodies, but the project materials do not say they have convened or who sits on them, one of them is bootstrapped at 1-of-1, and contract logic is upgradeable by RootPolicyBody [e]; no licence is published [c]. Regulatory (2): no token and no jurisdiction stated. Funding & Key-org Dependency (4): a single contributor and a single organisation, funding not stated [a][c]. Forking Viability (3): the specification and conformance vectors are published and wallet services and presses can be self-run [d], but with no licence grant the rights to reuse the code are unclear [c], and the protocol depends on Arbitrum One and IPFS [d][f]. Track Record (2): too new to show a record; no capture-favouring decision found [c].

entityAttributes.origins: A way for people who build community to share resources and build trust: membership credentials issued by communities themselves rather than by a platform, private by default, with proof of standing that does not depend on a central identity provider [a][c]
entityAttributes.database: Arbitrum One registry contract (a mutable pointer per card, press authorizations) plus append-only logs on IPFS; wallet services hold encrypted keyrings [d][f]
entityAttributes.queryLanguage: None. A card is found by deriving its registry address, keccak256 of its public key, then fetching its log from IPFS and decrypting it with a key derived from the same public key [d]
entityAttributes.dataFormats: A normative canonical serialization (spec Appendix A) with published conformance and versioning test vectors; card documents and log entries are encrypted JSON on IPFS; mcard:// URLs for offers [c][d]
entityAttributes.mobileSupport: Designed for it: mobile SDKs are listed as done and sub-card keys are held in device secure storage; there is no finished app [a][d]
entityAttributes.webSupport: A web SDK is listed as done, and a browser authentication flow (a request routed through CHAPI, or a future browser-native API) is specified; no finished frontend app [a][d]
entityAttributes.nativeApps: None yet: the frontend app is listed as not done [a]
entityAttributes.terms: Described as free to use and open source, but no licence file is published; presses pay a minimal fee, roughly $0.005, to create a card and may charge for cards [c]
entityAttributes.funds: Not stated by the project.
entityAttributes.basedOn: Arbitrum One (Stylus contracts, the RIP-7212 secp256r1 precompile); IPFS; ML-DSA-44 and ML-KEM post-quantum cryptography; passkeys and YubiKey backups; optional OHTTP [c][d]
entityAttributes.authenticationIdentity: Cards rather than accounts: a holder generates their own keypair on accepting a card, and the card's address is keccak256 of its public key. The master key stays cold; day-to-day signing uses device-held sub-card keys registered to it. A holder's cards are designed not to be linkable to one another [c][d]
entityAttributes.storageModel: Hybrid: registry pointers on Arbitrum One; encrypted append-only logs on IPFS (AES-256-GCM, content key derived from the card's public key); keyrings held encrypted by wallet services and replicated across a federation [d]
entityAttributes.interoperability: Its own credential design: the specification names no DIDs and lists a W3C Verifiable Credential compatibility layer only among future items [d]. Wallet-to-site requests are routed through CHAPI. The README says a verifier is available as an npm module and a Python library; an npm package named membership-card-verifier (version 0.0.1, 2026-07-12) exists but nothing links it to the project, and no Python package was found, so neither is confirmed [c]
entityAttributes.dataPortability: Cards are addressed by public key on a registry contract and logs sit on IPFS, so a card can be read by anyone holding its public key; keyrings are encrypted blobs replicated across wallet services, and the holder can recover them independently of the primary service via a YubiKey backup [d]
entityAttributes.governanceDecisionMaking: Protocol changes are designed to go through on-chain quorum bodies (see Governing Body); the site invites partners to take part in its governance, and today decisions rest with the author [a][e]
entityAttributes.identityStandards: None adopted: its own card and policy model, not W3C DIDs [d]
entityAttributes.didMethodsSupported: None.
entityAttributes.keyManagement: Passkey-encrypted master keys held in a keyring stored by the wallet service; sub-card keys in device secure storage (Secure Enclave or TPM) for routine signing; master keys used only to create sub-cards and rotate keys; rotation is deliberate, never automatic [d]
entityAttributes.credentialTypes: Cards: signed credentials defined by a policy (membership, roles, sub-cards, press authorizations), with typed fields and predicates and a three-digit update code for each log entry [d]
entityAttributes.verificationMethod: A verifier walks the chain of cards from the presented key back to a trusted root, checking each signature, that the issuer was authorized by policy, and that no revocation applies; signatures are ML-DSA-44, and press registry writes are verified on-chain with secp256r1 [c][d]
entityAttributes.privacyFeatures: Private by default: card content is encrypted on IPFS and readable only with the card's public key; a holder's cards are designed to be unlinkable; messages are end-to-end encrypted; optional OHTTP hides the requester's IP from the wallet service. The registry pointer and its updates are public on-chain [d]
entityAttributes.authenticationMethods: A wallet signs a statement or request with a card satisfying a predicate; the user approves each request, and a confirmation code ties the browser session to the signed response [d]
entityAttributes.revocationMechanism: Log entries with codes 800-999 revoke a card (quiet 8xx, loud 9xx) with an effective date; revocations cannot be erased, and standing is restored by issuing a successor card; presses can be revoked by the press registry body [d][e]
entityAttributes.agentTypesSupported: People, communities and organisations through cards, and services such as presses; any holder of a card key [c][d]
entityAttributes.walletClientTypes: Wallet services that hold encrypted keyrings and messaging endpoints, with web and mobile SDKs; anyone may run one [c][d]
entityAttributes.recoveryMechanisms: A YubiKey-based backup with a 72-hour window in which any registered cancellation credential can abort recovery, with notifications sent on all configured channels; recovery is independent of the primary wallet service. Guardian-quorum social recovery is a future item [d]
entityAttributes.complianceRegulations: Not stated by the project.
entityAttributes.credentialExchangeProtocols: The protocol's own signing and authentication request flow (CHAPI routing, a direct fetch, optional OHTTP) and its card-offer messages; no OpenID4VC or DIDComm [d]
entityAttributes.trustFramework: Chains of policy-defined cards back to a trusted root; the card protocol's presses sign only for policy adherence; a governance board is designed to update the protocol and address violations such as fraud [c][d][e]
entityAttributes.costModel: Low-cost writes: presses pay roughly $0.005 per card and may choose to charge for cards; no token [c]
entityAttributes.censorshipResistance: Moderate by design, unproven in practice: anyone can run wallet services and presses must be authorized on-chain, but press authorization is revocable by a governance body and the system depends on Arbitrum One and IPFS availability [c][d]
entityAttributes.protocolMaturityStandardization: Draft specification v0.4, "In Review", with conformance and versioning test vectors; not submitted to any standards body; mainnet contracts deployed; no independent audit yet [a][d][f]
entityAttributes.permissions: Press registry writes require an on-chain press authorization; issuing under a policy requires holding a press sub-card of that policy; anyone may run a wallet service and verify cards [d]

name: did:plc
description: A W3C-style DID method, "Public Ledger of Credentials", built for the AT Protocol (atproto) ecosystem but defined as a general DID method. A did:plc identifier is derived from the hash of its first signed operation, so it is self-certifying. Control rests in up to five priority-ordered rotation keys; each update is a signed operation that points to the previous one by hash, and a higher-priority key can overwrite a lower-priority one's operations within a 72-hour window. Operations are submitted to a central directory server that validates them, orders them and publishes the full log. No blockchain is used. The system gives accounts a persistent identifier that survives changes of name or service provider; in practice it identifies over 40 million atproto accounts, and the project names no non-atproto adopter. [a][b][c][d]
devStatus: Active. In production for atproto: the PLC Organization's site says it provides persistent identifiers to over 40 million accounts [d]. The method specification is at v0.3.0 (December 2025) [b], the reference repository was last updated on 2026-10-28 with 15 contributors, and a Go implementation is published beside it [c]; it is a registered method in the W3C DID Extensions registry [e]. The PLC Organization says it is still developing policies and building operational capacity [d]. Checked 2026-10-29.
owner: Bluesky Social PBC (original developer, 2022; copyright holder of the reference code); the PLC Organization, a small Swiss association founded in 2026, as neutral steward [a][c][d]
governingBody: PLC Organization (Swiss association, founded 2026, developing its policies) as neutral steward; Bluesky Social PBC as the original developer. The cited sources do not say who operates the directory at plc.directory today or how the steward is governed [a][d]
country: Switzerland (the PLC Organization, a Swiss association with a registered address in Zug) [d]
stack: TypeScript (reference library and directory server) and Go; DAG-CBOR operations with CIDs; ECDSA-SHA256 over secp256k1 or P-256; did:key encoding of keys; HTTP API described by an OpenAPI schema [a][b][c]
license: Permissive (dual MIT / Apache-2.0, at the user's option; copyright 2022-2026 Bluesky Social PBC). https://github.com/did-method-plc/did-method-plc (TypeScript reference implementation and directory server); https://github.com/did-method-plc/go-didplc (Go implementation, Apache-2.0) [c]
funding: Not stated by the project.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3), provisional, from public documentation only. Governance & Legal Control (3): the method was written by Bluesky Social PBC and a single central directory server orders and publishes every operation, which the specification itself says requires trust (it can refuse operations or serve the wrong fork after a dispute) [b]; stewardship is moving to a neutral Swiss association founded in 2026 that says it is still developing its policies [d], and the code is dual MIT / Apache-2.0 [c]. Regulatory (2): no token; the steward is a Swiss association [d]. Funding & Key-org Dependency (4): the project describes no funding for the new steward and nearly all registered identifiers belong to one ecosystem built by one company [a][d]. Forking Viability (3): the code, the full operation log and an export API are public and there are two implementations [a][c], but identifiers resolve through the directory's ordering and no second directory is described [b]. Track Record (2): developed since 2022 and in production at scale, with no capture-favouring decision found, and the move to a neutral steward points the other way [a][d].

name: did:vh
description: "DID + Verifiable History": a DID method that is the location-independent sibling of did:webvh. A did:vh identifier is only the method prefix and a self-certifying identifier (SCID) derived from the DID's first log entry, so it contains no domain name or path and is not tied to any place where its log is published. It specialises the VH-Log specification: the DID document's history is a hash-chained, signed log (did.jsonl) with optional pre-rotation of keys, witnesses and watchers. Because the DID names no location, a resolver is handed the log (or a reference to it) rather than fetching it from a well-known URL, and the SCID proves the log is the authentic history wherever it came from. Unlike did:webvh it drops the DID-to-HTTPS transformation, the portability parameter and the implicit #files and #whois services. Currently an early draft by a single editor. [a][b][c]
devStatus: Draft. The specification is an Editors Draft, v0.1, and its changelog calls v0.1 "Pre-Draft" [a]; no reference implementation or test suite is linked from it, the repository has one contributor and four commits, and it is not in the W3C DID Extensions registry (the registry's methods directory has no entry) [a][b][e]. The spec says did:webvh implementations should be able to support it by swapping the resolution step [a]. Checked 2026-10-29.
owner: No organization is named; the specification lists a single editor and is developed in a personal GitHub repository [a][b]
governingBody: None named. Developed in the open by a single editor; related specifications VH-Log and did:webvh are separate projects [a][b]
stack: JSON Lines DID log (did.jsonl) of signed, hash-chained entries; witness proofs in did-witness.json; did:key for witness identifiers; cryptographic agility through versioned parameters [a][c]
license: The specification is under the W3C Patent Policy (2004) terms and any sample or reference code in the repository is Apache-2.0, per the repository's licence file, which inherits them from the Decentralized Identity Foundation project charter [d]. https://github.com/swcurran/didvh [b]
funding: Not stated by the project.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3), provisional, from public documentation only. Governance & Legal Control (3): the specification has a single editor and no named hosting organization or standards body, and no governance process is documented [a][b]; the licence is permissive and inherited from a foundation charter [d]. name: Loro
description: A CRDT (conflict-free replicated data type) library for local-first, real-time collaborative software. An application models its state as Loro's JSON-like collaborative types (text with Fugue-based merging, rich text, movable lists, movable trees, last-write-wins maps and counters); any number of peers edit independently and offline, export their updates as bytes, send them over any channel, and import the other side's updates to converge on the same state. Loro also keeps the full editing history, so a document can be time-travelled or branched like a version-controlled repository, and a shallow snapshot lets a document drop old history the way a shallow git clone does. It is a library, not a network: the project supplies the data structures and encoding, and the application chooses the transport. Available in Rust, JavaScript (via WebAssembly) and Swift, with bindings for other languages in a separate repository [a][b][c][d].
devStatus: Active. Loro 1.0 has been announced and the most recent release, loro-crdt 1.17.1, was published on 2026-10-22; the repository's last change was on 2026-10-23, with over 260 commits in the past year and 43 contributors, though one founder authored about three quarters of the latest 100 commits [c][e]. The project's site lists commercial and hobby products using it (for example a computational-notebook tool and a chat app) in user testimonials; these are the project's own claims [a]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: cr-sqlite
description: cr-sqlite is a run-time loadable extension for SQLite (and libSQL) that lets separate copies of a database, each of which has taken independent writes while offline, be merged without conflict. A table is upgraded into a 'conflict-free replicated relation' with one function call; the extension then exposes a virtual table of changes that one peer can read and another can apply, and applies column-level conflict resolution so every replica converges. The project calls this 'like Git, for your data'. It does not include networking: the application moves change sets between devices or a server by whatever means it likes. It is one component of the broader Vulcan project from Vulcan Labs, which also lists a reactive-query engine and a web stack built on SQLite as a collaborative application file format [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active, with light maintenance. The latest release, v0.16.3, dates from 2024-01-17 and the pre-1.0 version number is unchanged since [c]. name: PouchDB
description: An open-source JavaScript database inspired by Apache CouchDB, designed to run inside the browser so that web applications work as well offline as online. Applications store JSON documents in a local database; PouchDB replicates them, in either direction and continuously if wanted, with CouchDB or any server that speaks the CouchDB replication protocol, and resolves conflicts using CouchDB's revision model. It is not a self-contained storage engine but a CouchDB-style layer over other stores: by default it uses IndexedDB in the browser and LevelDB in Node.js, with other adapters available. The project is currently an Apache Software Foundation Incubator podling [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active, in wide production use for offline-first web applications. The latest release, 9.0.0, was published on 2024-06-21; development resumed visibly in 2026, with over 90 commits between March and June 2026 [a][c]. The ASF Incubator lists it as a podling still working through incubation requirements, so it has not yet graduated to a top-level project [d]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Apache CouchDB
description: An open-source NoSQL document database with an HTTP/JSON API, built for reliability and for multi-primary sync that scales from large clusters down to mobile and browser clients. Any CouchDB database, on a server or a device, can replicate with any other over the documented CouchDB Replication Protocol, which synchronises JSON documents between two peers over HTTP/1.1 using the public REST API and the project's multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) model; conflicting edits are detected through revision trees rather than merged automatically. CouchDB is the reference implementation of that protocol, which PouchDB and other tools reuse. It is a project of the Apache Software Foundation [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active, in wide production use. Version 3.5.3 was released on 2026-10-12 and the repository's last change was on 2026-10-29, with over 500 commits in the past year and mailing-list and chat support [a][c]. Checked 2026-10-29.

description: A local-first, reactive NoSQL database for JavaScript applications. RxDB replicates to existing backends (the project lists replication with CouchDB, GraphQL, REST, WebRTC, and several hosted services, among others), has plugins for conflict handling, CRDT-style conflict resolution, encryption, schema validation and migration, and swaps its storage engine to suit the runtime. name: UCAN
description: User Controlled Authorization Network: a specification for authorization that is public-key verifiable, delegable and openly extensible, with no central authority needed to check a permission. A UCAN is a signed token in which one party, identified by a decentralized identifier (DID), grants a capability over a resource to another and may allow that party to pass it on in narrower form; a chain of such tokens is the proof that a request is authorised, and anyone can verify the chain offline. The specification is split into sub-specifications for delegation, invocation, promise and revocation. It was designed for local-first and peer-to-peer settings and positions itself as a successor to access control lists and as an authorization layer for applications and AI agents [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active. The specification README is at version 1.0.0 although the latest repository tag is v1.0-rc.1; the repository was last changed on 2026-10-22 and has 16 contributors, one of whom made about half of the commits [c][d]. Implementations and a website with a UCAN inspector are listed by the project [a]. The cited sources give no independent statement of production deployments; the Active rating rests on the live specification work and the listed libraries. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Eclipse Biscuit
description: An authorization token with decentralized verification, offline attenuation and policy enforcement based on a logic language (Datalog). A Biscuit is signed with public-key cryptography so any service that knows the public key can verify it, and the holder can derive a new token with fewer rights, for instance a read-only or time-limited one, without contacting the issuer. Authorization policies are written in Datalog and can be supplied by the verifying application or carried by the token. Every token has unique revocation identifiers that reject it and all tokens attenuated from it. It suits capability-based authorization but can also express access control lists. Implementations exist in Rust, Haskell, Go, Java, JavaScript and WebAssembly, C, Python and C#; it is an Eclipse Foundation project [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active. Version 3.3 of the specification and tooling was released on 2025-08-06 and the Rust library (biscuit-auth 6.0.0, 2025-07-16) was changed on the day of checking; the Eclipse project page lists it as Incubating [b][c]. The README says the project is deploying to real-world use cases (an Apache Pulsar integration at Clever Cloud) and is still looking for an audit of the token's design and implementations, so production use is real but limited and unaudited [c]. The specification repository itself had no commits since October 2025 [c]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: AnonCreds
description: Anonymous Credentials: a verifiable-credential format that uses zero-knowledge proofs, so a holder can prove claims from credentials without revealing the credentials or a correlatable identifier. An issuer publishes a schema and a credential definition (with a public key), signs a credential for a holder, and can publish a revocation registry; the holder later produces a proof that discloses only chosen attributes or predicates (for example 'over 18') and proves the credential is not revoked, linking multiple credentials through a hidden master secret. The specification formalises an implementation in use since 2017, first in Hyperledger Indy and now the Hyperledger AnonCreds project, now hosted at the LF Decentralized Trust. The v1.0 draft aims to be ledger-agnostic [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active. The specification says the extensive use of AnonCreds around the world has made it a de facto standard for ZKP-based verifiable credentials; the specification itself is a v1.0 Draft and the reference library anoncreds-rs was released as v0.2.3 on 2025-11-13 [a][d]. The repositories moved to the new 'anoncreds' GitHub organisation in January 2026 and the specification repository was last changed on 2026-01-13, so recent activity is modest [b][d]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Privacy Pass
description: A privacy-preserving authorization protocol that lets a client prove it has passed some check, such as solving a challenge or being a legitimate user of a device, without being tracked across requests. A server issues tokens that are cryptographically blinded, so that when a token is later redeemed the issuer cannot link it to the issuance. It is now an IETF standards-track family: RFC 9576 describes the architecture, RFC 9577 the HTTP authentication scheme, and RFC 9578 the issuance protocols (published June 2024). The original deployment was a browser extension that let people skip CAPTCHA challenges at sites behind Cloudflare [a][b][c][d].
devStatus: Active, in production use: the project's site says Cloudflare supports it to let users redeem passes instead of solving CAPTCHAs, and the protocol family was published as RFCs 9576, 9577 and 9578 in June 2024 [a][b][c][d]. The browser extension is a legacy implementation; the working group's draft repository was last changed in May 2024 [a][e]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Semaphore
description: A zero-knowledge protocol for anonymous interactions: a user proves they are a member of a group, and sends a signal such as a vote or endorsement, without revealing which member they are. Group membership is a Merkle tree of identity commitments; a Semaphore proof shows knowledge of a leaf in the tree and ties the signal to a nullifier that stops the same member from signalling twice in the same context. Semaphore is described as a generic privacy layer, with circuits, Solidity contracts for on-chain verification, and JavaScript libraries for creating and verifying proofs off-chain. It is developed by Privacy & Scaling Explorations, a team supported by the Ethereum Foundation, and Semaphore V4 has been released [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active, in production use by projects that list themselves on the Semaphore site, including World ID (Worldcoin), which the site names, plus anonymous-voting and identity tools [a]. The latest release, v4.14.5, was published on 2026-10-17 and the repository was last changed on that date, with 77 contributors [d]. Checked 2026-10-29.
owner: Privacy & Scaling Explorations (PSE), a team supported by the Ethereum Foundation; the repository is under the semaphore-protocol organisation, with one contributor responsible for about two thirds of the latest commits [a][b][d]
governingBody: Privacy & Scaling Explorations (PSE), supported by the Ethereum Foundation; no formal governance document was found in the cited sources [a][b]
stack: Circom circuits (built with circomkit); Solidity contracts for on-chain verification and groups on EVM chains; JavaScript packages for identity, group and proof; Semaphore V4 uses EdDSA identities and LeanIMT groups, as the RLN V3 README describes [b][c]
license: Permissive (MIT). https://github.com/semaphore-protocol/semaphore (circuits, Solidity contracts, JavaScript packages) [b][d]
funding: Supported by the Ethereum Foundation through the PSE team [a][b]

name: RLN (Rate-Limiting Nullifier)
description: A zero-knowledge gadget for spam prevention in anonymous environments. In an application where users are anonymous, nothing stops one user from sending unlimited messages, and nobody can be removed because nobody can be identified. RLN lets a member prove, in zero knowledge, that they belong to a registered group and are within a rate limit; if they exceed it, the extra proof reveals enough of their secret (through Shamir's Secret Sharing) for others to recover it and remove them, optionally taking a stake. It works in three phases: registration, interaction and withdrawal or slashing. It is described as part of Privacy & Scaling Explorations (PSE), a team supported by the Ethereum Foundation, and implementations are used as the spam-protection layer for messaging protocols [a][b][c].
devStatus: Beta. A formal specification, documentation, circuits, contracts and a Rust implementation (zerokit) exist; zerokit released v3.0.0 on 2026-08-04 and RLN V3, built on Semaphore V4, was last changed in May 2026, while most of the RLN organisation's other repositories have had no commits since 2023-2024 [d][e][f]. The cited sources do not confirm that RLN secures a production network today; the documentation describes its use as a spam-protection layer for messaging protocols. Checked 2026-10-29.

governingBody: Privacy & Scaling Explorations (PSE) team, supported by the Ethereum Foundation; no formal governance body is described [a]

name: SimpleX Network
description: A messaging network, and the SimpleX Chat apps built on it, that uses no user identifiers of any kind: no phone number, username or account ID. Two people connect through one-time invitation links or QR codes, and each conversation runs over separate, unidirectional message queues held on relay servers (SMP servers), with files on separate file servers (XFTP). Relays see only queue addresses, not who is talking to whom, and only the client devices hold information about users, contacts and groups, which the project says avoids the metadata exposure of federated networks. Messages use double-ratchet end-to-end encryption with an additional encryption layer. Anyone can run a relay, and the apps ship with preset relay operators, including SimpleX Chat Ltd and Flux. The apps run on iOS, Android and desktop, and there is a terminal app [a][b].
devStatus: Active. Version 7.0.3 was released on 2026-09-26 and the repository was changed on 2026-10-21; it has a large issue backlog (about 1,300 open) and many contributors. Trail of Bits did an implementation security assessment of the cryptography and networking in October 2022 and a cryptographic review of the protocols in July 2024, per the project [a][d]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Briar
description: A messaging app for activists, journalists and anyone who needs a safe and robust way to communicate. Unlike conventional messengers it has no central server: messages are synchronised directly between users' devices. If the internet is down, Briar can sync over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or memory cards; if it is up, it syncs over the Tor network to hide who is talking to whom. Briar Mailbox lets users who are online at different times exchange messages. Alongside private messaging it offers public forums and blogs, each user's contact list is encrypted and stored on their own device, and all communication between devices is end-to-end encrypted. Briar is for Android, with a desktop version in development [a][b].
devStatus: Active. Version 1.5.23 was prepared on 2026-10-27, the latest commit that day, and the repository has a small number of open issues. The project ships reproducible builds so published APKs can be checked against the source [a][c]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Session
description: A private messaging app and network that protects metadata as well as content. Messages are end-to-end encrypted with libsodium and routed through a decentralised onion-routing network the project calls onion requests, so that no single server knows both the origin and the destination of a message; identities are anonymous and messages are stored in swarms of network nodes until collected. The app runs on mobile and desktop, supports one-to-one and group messages, and the project says contributors are working on Session Protocol V2, which plans post-quantum cryptography. It is stewarded by the Session Technology Foundation, a Swiss foundation without shareholders, and the site lists a Session token [a][b][c].

name: Syncthing
description: A continuous file synchronisation program that keeps folders identical across two or more computers in real time, directly between devices and with no central server. Devices are identified by a cryptographic certificate fingerprint (the Device ID); only devices a user has explicitly accepted can connect, and all traffic is encrypted with TLS including forward secrecy. Devices find each other on the local network or, optionally, through global discovery servers, and can fall back to community relay servers when no direct connection is possible. The protocol is a documented specification, the code is open source and development is public. It is maintained under the Syncthing Foundation, a registered Swedish non-profit foundation [a][b][c].

name: Eclipse Zenoh
description: A pub/sub/query protocol that unifies data in motion, data at rest and computation. It combines publish/subscribe with geo-distributed storage, queries and computations, while keeping time and space efficiency the project describes as well beyond mainstream stacks, with a five-byte wire overhead. Applications use first-class abstractions for pub/sub, storages and queryables, with several levels of reliability, dynamic discovery, fragmentation and batching. The Rust crate is the reference implementation of the protocol and the libraries for other languages are bindings to it, apart from a pure-C implementation for microcontrollers (zenoh-pico). It is an incubating project of the Eclipse Foundation [a][b][c].

name: Signal Protocol / libsignal
description: The cryptographic protocol suite behind the Signal messenger, published as the libsignal library. It contains the Signal protocol, including the Double Ratchet algorithm, with Rust implementations exposed as Java, Swift and TypeScript libraries, plus the cryptographic primitives and supporting components Signal uses: device-to-device transfer, remote attestation of server enclaves, zero-knowledge group credentials (zkgroup and zkcredential), usernames, and PIN-based secure value recovery keys. The repository is used by the official Signal clients and servers; the project says use outside Signal is unsupported and that APIs and implementations may change without notice. The messenger itself is a service run by the Signal Technology Foundation [a][b].

name: Secure Scuttlebutt (SSB)
description: A decentralised, peer-to-peer social network and protocol in which each user keeps an append-only log of signed messages on their own device and syncs with peers by gossip, including over a local network without internet access. Because each log is an unforgeable feed, peers need not be trusted and can pass on other peers' logs and files; the original server software describes itself as a peer-to-peer log store used as a database, identity provider and messaging system, with global replication, file synchronisation and end-to-end encrypted messages. The protocol is documented in a community guide. The project is run by the Secure Scuttlebutt Consortium; the main clients (Patchwork, then Manyverse) and the original server have stopped receiving updates, and the lightweight tinySSB variant is a separate entry in this matrix [a][b][c].
devStatus: Unmaintained. The original server's last commit was in June 2022 and its last release in December 2018; the Patchwork client repository is archived (last pushed May 2021); the Manyverse mobile client's latest release (v0.2407.28-beta) and its last push were both in August 2024; ssb-db2 was last pushed in April 2024 [b][c][d]. Only the protocol guide (last pushed March 2026) and the separate tinySSB project (last pushed July 2026) show recent activity [e][f]. The network reached real use by many people; the Scuttlebutt site still invites newcomers to start and read the docs [a]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: OpenMLS
description: A Rust implementation of the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol as specified in RFC 9420. It is a software library meant to be a building block for applications that need end-to-end encryption of group messages, with an interface that hides the complexity of the underlying cryptography. OpenMLS does not implement its own primitives: it relies on pluggable cryptography providers (a RustCrypto-based one and a libcrux-based one) and storage providers (in-memory, SQLite and others). It supports three ciphersuites, builds for several platforms including WebAssembly, and provides an interoperability client and a delivery-service example. It is the reference-style Rust implementation of the standard that has its own entry in this matrix as MLS (Messaging Layer Security) [a].
devStatus: Beta. name: p2panda
description: A modular toolkit of Rust crates for building privacy-respecting, secure local-first applications. Instead of one framework, p2panda offers separate libraries for networking and discovery, local-first sync of append-only logs, blob transfer, storage, stream processing, group encryption with post-compromise security, and decentralised group management with per-member permissions, so projects pick only what they need. Many crates work on raw bytes and are compatible with any CRDT. It builds on existing libraries such as iroh and on standards including BLAKE3, Ed25519, CBOR, TLS and QUIC. Its design is 'broadcast-only' at heart, so data can travel over unreliable or unconventional media, including shortwave, packet radio, Bluetooth Low Energy, LoRa or a USB stick. The README says the library is under active development and its APIs are not yet stable for production [a][b].
devStatus: Alpha. The project's own news posts describe ongoing design work on access control and sync [b]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: TACo (Threshold Access Control)
description: A decentralised access-control layer: end-to-end encrypted data sharing and automation without a central authority that could deny service or decrypt user data. Data is encrypted to a public key, and a threshold of independently operated TACo nodes each check that a requester meets user-authored, programmable conditions (for example 'share my archive with journalists if I do not check in over seven days') before releasing a fragment of decryption material, so no single node can open the data. An experimental variant, Threshold Action Control, does conditions-based signing. Applications integrate through a software development kit, and the node network was operated by independent, collateralised nodes. The NuCypher organisation that built it is no longer active; the project is now under the stewardship of the World Ethical Data Foundation, and a relaunch centred on a 'Privacy Coalition' has been announced [a][b][c].
devStatus: Unmaintained, with a relaunch announced. The repository README opens with an 'Inactive Project' banner (added 2026-05-24): the NuCypher organisation 'is no longer active and will not continue development or maintenance of this code base', and the original project is expected to be forked and relaunched by the World Ethical Data Forum in the second half of 2026 with a coalition of node operators; the documentation says operators may keep running node clients in the interim and that a stable service will be relaunched in Q3 2026 [a][b]. The README describes the network as having been in production ('live, well-collateralised and battle-tested'). The cited sources show no evidence that the relaunch has happened. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Lokinet
description: An anonymous, decentralised, IP-based overlay network. Lokinet is the reference implementation of LLARP, the low latency anonymous routing protocol, a layer 3 onion-routing protocol, so that ordinary applications can use it without being rewritten. Traffic is onion-routed and Lokinet hides both a user's IP address and the IP addresses they connect to; the network is run by a decentralised set of staked nodes, and it can host services reachable only inside the network. Clients are available for Windows and Linux, with macOS and mobile clients described as in development. The project's site says nobody can shut it down and nobody can spy on users, which are the project's own claims [a][b].
devStatus: Active, with slowing maintenance. The latest release, v0.9.14, was published on 2025-07-28; almost all of the latest 100 commits fall in September and October 2025 and the only later commit (July 2026) updated the package-signing key; open issues are still being filed, including a proposal to add payments to the exit marketplace (August 2026) [b]. The site describes the network as run by staked nodes and offers Windows and Linux clients [a]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Nym
description: A privacy platform built around a mixnet: a network of mix nodes that shuffle fixed-size Sphinx packets and add timing noise, so that network observers cannot link who is communicating with whom even if they can watch all traffic. Nodes run by decentralised operators act as mixnodes, entry gateways (a kind of mailbox that removes the need for direct delivery to devices that are offline or behind firewalls) and exit gateways that route data to the internet; the platform also includes clients, a SOCKS5 proxy, a wallet and a command-line tool, and the commercial NymVPN app uses the network. Network economics, operator rewards and validator rewards follow a published whitepaper that includes a NYM token with an initial reward pool of 250 million tokens [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active, in production use. A new binary release (nym-binaries-v2026.21-hanoi) was published on 2026-10-28 and the repository was changed on 2026-10-29, with about 150 open issues and a commercial VPN product built on the network [a][b]. Checked 2026-10-29.

name: Katzenpost
description: A free and open-source post-quantum mix network that hides who is talking to whom from network-level observers, including adversaries who record traffic today to decrypt on a future quantum computer. A mix network is made of mix nodes that act as cryptographic packet-switching routers, mixing many messages together, transforming them and adding shuffling or delay so that incoming and outgoing messages cannot be linked. Katzenpost also provides Pigeonhole, an anonymous storage layer on top of the mixnet in which applications exchange encrypted, append-only streams of fixed-size padded boxes sharded across replicas and governed by write and read capabilities, with thin clients in Go, Rust and Python and a Qt group-chat client. Its design is described in a paper on the Echomix anonymity system, and a public Katzenpost network called Namenlos is listed as coming next [a][b].
devStatus: Alpha. The latest tag is v0.0.107 and the repository was changed on 2026-10-29, with about nine tenths of the latest 100 commits by one contributor; the project's site lists Pigeonhole, the katzenqt client and the client daemon as available to build from source, and pre-built packages and a public network (Namenlos) as 'coming next', so no public network is offered yet [a][b]. name: Garage
description: An S3-compatible object store for small, self-hosted, geo-distributed deployments, designed so that a cluster can run outside datacentres on whatever second-hand machines are available. Each chunk of data is replicated in three zones; the cluster tolerates network failures, latency, disk failures and operator error; it ships as a single dependency-free binary and runs on modest hardware (any x86_64 CPU of the last ten years, ARMv7 or ARMv8, 1 GB of RAM, 16 GB of disk, 200 ms latency or less). It implements the Amazon S3 API so many applications already work with it, and it draws on research on Dynamo, conflict-free replicated data types and Maglev. It is run and funded as a community and public-funding project and is not a network anyone can join: the operator of a cluster decides who the nodes are [a][b].

name: Elohim Protocol
description: A peer-to-peer substrate for content that carries its own knowledge, value and governance. Its unit is the Elohim Protocol Record (EPR): a deterministically encoded (DAG-CBOR) record with a CIDv1 content address and a signed envelope that says what the content is, who stewards it and what economic flows attach to it, and which governance decides how far it may travel (its 'reach', a ladder from private to commons). Holochain 0.7, in a pinned fork, is the 'notary floor': five DNAs hold the rules for identity, shared content, community proposals and judgments, node capacity and a node registry. A storage sidecar moves content-addressed bytes between peers over libp2p and iroh, and 'doorways' project the network to ordinary browsers over HTTP and DNS, so people without a node can take part; a person can start hosted by a doorway and move to their own device later. Economics are modelled as ValueFlows / REA events rather than a token. The design also includes AI agents bound by a written constitution and acting under each person's authorisation. The project's own status statement of September 2026 separates what runs today, a test household mesh and a small alpha fleet of doorways, storage and conductors, from what is designed but not yet running, which includes the agent runtime [a][b][c].
devStatus: Alpha. The README's 'What runs today (September 2026)' section lists what runs: a test household mesh and an alpha fleet of doorways, storage and conductors serving the apps at alpha.elohim.host, the Visitor and Hosted participation stages, a first stage of an authoring gate on the storage path, and the repository's own governance rules. It lists as designed but not yet running: the agent runtime (the crate exists, no service runs it), reach gated by standing, attestation gates, the feed protocol and the AT Protocol and ActivityPub bridges. Production deploys are paused; the desktop steward app and the node runtime build from source and no packaged release is linked; the repository has no GitHub releases. One developer account authors nearly all commits (11,345 of about 11,630) and AI-assistant commits are openly recorded. Checked 2026-10-29 [a][b].

Declared in the crate manifests: CAL-1.0 for the EPR codec and the ValueFlows / REA crates; AGPL-3.0 for the storage sidecar and the SDK crate; Apache-2.0 for the doorway, eprfs, the steward node, the compute types and as the Rust workspace default; MIT OR Apache-2.0 for the relay beacon. name: Nondominium
description: A resource-sharing application built on Holochain and the ValueFlows standard. Agents create, hold and transfer shared resources called Nondominium Objects (NDOs), which the project intends to be organisation-agnostic. Each NDO has a permanent identity anchor (name, initiator, lifecycle stage, property regime and resource nature) and moves through ten lifecycle stages checked by the integrity rules. People enter through a permissionless Lobby, join Groups by invite link, each Group being its own cloned DHT network, and browse and create NDOs inside them; each NDO is itself a cloned Holochain cell whose DNA hash is its identity. Economic events are recorded through a bundled hREA DNA, and a reputation system based on Private Participation Receipts (PPRs) is specified. The project's own changelog states that governance-as-operator, PPR wiring, economic processes (use, transport, storage, repair) and role promotion are designed but not implemented in the first pilot release, so reputation is currently inert. It is a venture of the Sensorica open value network, aimed at helping open-hardware communities and traditional organisations share resources [a][b][c][d].
devStatus: WIP. The changelog calls version 0.1.0 an unreleased 'internal Sensorica pilot with a limited demo cohort, not a public launch'; no tag or release exists. What is built is a peer mesh in which agents share a Group and an NDO over a live DHT, with Lobby and Group DNAs, NDO identity and lifecycle, and a three-level web UI. The changelog and the project's implementation-status document list what is not built: governance as operator, PPR issuance wiring, economic processes, role promotion, capability-based private data sharing and NDO layers 1 and 2; the release targets Holochain 0.6. The Sensorica page calls the status 'prototyping and funding stage', and one architecture document calls the design 'production-ready', which the changelog contradicts, so the changelog is followed here. About 240 commits, almost all by two developers; last change 2026-10-28; 58 open issues. Checked 2026-10-29 [a][b][c][d][e][h].

The Sensorica site states that all software developed by its network is licensed GNU AGPL, which conflicts with the repository text. https://github.com/sensorica/nondominium [a][b][f]
funding: Public funding and crowdfunding are the stated short-term model; the project page records a failed NGI Assure application in 2023 and a crowdfunding effort not yet launched, and offers contributors a share of grants through Sensorica's contribution logging [b]

name: JLINC
description: A protocol for sharing data under a signed agreement on the terms of sharing. Its core ideas are Verifiable Contractual Agreements, signed by the DIDs of the parties, and Zero-Knowledge Auditing, in which each party keeps a signed hash of the agreed record so that later use of the data can be audited without exposing the data itself. The protocol is at version 10 and uses a W3C-style DID document for each party, with its own did:jlinc DID method [a][b].

name: Spritely Goblins
description: A distributed object programming environment from the Spritely Institute: a library, not a language, for writing programs as objects (actors) that follow object-capability security, run transactionally in local vats, and can live anywhere on a network. It has implementations for Guile and Racket, persistence that can serialize a whole live object graph, and speaks OCapN, the draft Object Capability Network protocol that other implementations such as Endo and DObjects also follow [a][b][c].

name: Real Life Trust Protocol (RLTP)
description: A family of specifications, schemas and test vectors for a decentralized trust protocol rooted in encounters between people, published by the Real Life Organisation. It is layered: identity (a key-derived anchor per person and pairwise anchors), encounter (a ceremony in which two people confirm they met), trust, and access (groups as places, with policy and epochs), with delivery and replication kept behind ports. It follows the Decentralized Trust Graph work at Trust Over IP, binds Trust Spanning Protocol through a mediator adapter, and is the third generation of a protocol whose second generation runs in the Web of Trust app. Every document is an Editor's Draft [a][b][c].

entityAttributes.didMethodsSupported: did:key only (the anchor); did:key identifiers cannot rotate, so the community anchor rotates through generations with a pre-committed next key; did:peer:2 appears only in an informative interoperability check [b]
entityAttributes.keyManagement: Keys derived from a 12 or 24-word BIP-39 phrase with HKDF-SHA-256 for Ed25519 signing and X25519 agreement; pre-rotation binding of the next anchor key; recovery must not require a custodian of key material [b]
entityAttributes.credentialTypes: Encounter credentials and cards (immutable), relationship credentials in the Decentralized Trust Graph form, trust and personhood predicates (draft) [a][b]
entityAttributes.verificationMethod: Data Integrity proofs (eddsa-jcs-2022) over JCS-canonicalized JSON with SHA-256; challenge-response in the encounter ceremony [b]
entityAttributes.privacyFeatures: Pairwise anchors aim for unlinkability, which the identity specification says holds until disclosed or stolen; storage services see sealed envelopes, sizes and timing [b]
entityAttributes.authenticationMethods: An in-person encounter ceremony with a fresh single-use challenge per enactment, confirmed by both parties; a fresh pair anchor per enactment [b]
entityAttributes.revocationMechanism: Device revocation per group in the access layer; encounter credentials are immutable and not revocable; revocation of the person's anchor is not stated [b]
entityAttributes.agentTypesSupported: People and their devices; groups as places; delivery services and mediators [a][b]
entityAttributes.walletClientTypes: The second-generation Web of Trust app (production); a third-generation app is in preparation; browser simulators [a][c]
entityAttributes.recoveryMechanisms: The recovery phrase restores keys, not state; losing the phrase is cryptographically final; restoring state needs an encrypted copy at a storage service [b]
entityAttributes.complianceRegulations: None claimed: the encounter specification states that the protocol does not prove personhood; GDPR and eIDAS are not stated in the layers read [b]
entityAttributes.credentialExchangeProtocols: Delivery through contracts behind ports; the first adapter binds Trust Spanning Protocol through the VTI mediator; Trust Tasks follow the Decentralized Trust Graph framework [a]
entityAttributes.trustFramework: Trust grows from verified in-person encounters recorded as credentials, then a trust layer and personhood predicates (drafts); no accredited trust framework is stated [a][b]
entityAttributes.costModel: Free specification and open-source code; no commercial terms stated [a]
entityAttributes.censorshipResistance: Not stated by the project; the specification names no transport and relies on delivery adapters [a]
entityAttributes.protocolMaturityStandardization: Editor's Drafts (Identity 0.55.0-draft, Encounter 0.32.0-draft, dated 2026-10-27; Access 0.58, Delivery Contract 0.85); aligned with, but not submitted to, a standards body [a][b]
entityAttributes.permissions: Open: CC BY 4.0 specification text; Apache-2.0 code [a]

name: GEB Network
description: A live public blockchain network (the renamed BEVM(λ), a Bitcoin-linked EVM chain built on Substrate) whose project describes it as a reality-perceiving complex adaptive system of cooperating 'Agere' subsystems. Accounts are bound to Bitcoin addresses, bitcoin is used as the gas unit, and a reputation-based 'Agere' consensus layer is described in its white paper. The mainnet produces a block about every six seconds and has a public block explorer, but current traffic is very light. This is not Reflexer's GEB stablecoin framework [a][b][c].
devStatus: Active (the mainnet produces blocks and has a public explorer; releases are binaries only, the latest v0.4.3 of December 2025, and the main repository's source history stops in January 2025; traffic is currently very light) [a][b][c]
devStatusNote: Active (the mainnet produces blocks and has a public explorer; releases are binaries only, the latest v0.4.3 of December 2025, and the main repository's source history stops in January 2025; traffic is currently very light) [a][b][c]
owner: Not stated by the project.
governingBody: Not stated by the project.
stack: Rust (Substrate / Polkadot SDK fork with an EVM layer from Frontier); Blockscout explorer; Solidity contracts; Docker images for validator and sync nodes (x86_64) [a][b]
license: Mixed by repository: the main chain code is GPL-3.0; some forks are Apache-2.0 or MIT; the white paper repository states no licence; Agere-Consensus reports 'other'. The v0.4.3 release says the published source has not been synchronized to the release and provides binaries only [a][b]
funding: Not stated by the project.
captureRiskReasoning: Overall Moderate (3), provisional, from public documentation only. Governance & Legal Control (4): no operator, legal entity or governance process is stated, and the validator set is not published [a]. Regulatory (3): a chain with a native-gas bitcoin bridge, an airdrop and token transfers carries custody and securities questions even though none is stated [a][c]. Funding & Key-org Dependency (4): funding is not stated [a]. Forking Viability (3): GPL-3.0 code, but releases are binaries and the source is not synchronized to them [b]. Track Record (3): a chain running since at least 2023 with over 14 million blocks, but light current use [c]. Mean 3.4 → 3.
